articles.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
articles.author: Mina al-Lami
articles.body_markdown:
**Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.**

The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.

"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.

It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?

## Significant defeats

Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.

Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).

He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.

Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.

That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.

But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".

For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.

## A means to an end?

Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".

But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.

Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.

And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.

It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.

In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.

There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.

Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."

## Taliban v Sharaa

The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.

Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.

Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.

The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.

Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.

There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.

With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.

The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".

That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.

## History lessons

Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.

The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

- Published30 October
- Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
- Published16 November
- Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?
- Published29 October

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.

Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" â a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.

"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.

But not everyone is changing tactics.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.

And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.

Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.

The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

articles.title: At this Little Free Bakery in Austin, neighbors come for the pastries and stay for community connection
articles.author: Wynne Davis
articles.body_markdown:
**AUSTIN, Texas—** When lines form in parks they're usually for the playground. Kids taking turns on slides. Runners waiting to get a drink from a water fountain. But the line that forms in the Bruning Green park in Austin's North Loop neighborhood happens only once a month, always on the first Sunday, and includes people of all ages. They're all here for Sarah Mason's bakery.

Unlike other bakeries in town where a pastry can run upwards of $7, everything here is free.

Mason's popup is one of countless Little Free Bakeries across the country. The idea is similar to Little Free Libraries, the small boxes that are often set up in front yards where passersby can leave or take a book as they please. Instead of books, it's baked goods that are up for grabs.

The bakers behind these Little Free Bakeries make everything from classic chocolate chip cookies to croissants all at no cost to their neighbors. Some have different reasons for starting than others, but what many inadvertently created is a space for their community to come together and get to know one another.

Mason started the Free Bakery North Loop last September when she was working on improving her technical pastry skills. She was handing out baked goods at her job as an office leasing representative for WeWork, but soon she had more than she could give away.

For her first free bakery, Mason made around 150 items, ranging from coconut chocolate chip cookies to bacon cheddar chive scones.

She thought people would happen upon the event as they were walking through the neighborhood. But just in case, she posted on social media. That post took off and since then there has always been a line.

"I have a friend who jokes that waiting in the line is the most fun part, because everyone's excited and talking about what they're going to get when they get to the front of the line and you can meet people," Mason said.

People love a free treat, but Mason said she is pleasantly surprised at how many people stick around and hang out.

"It was unexpected," she said. "My observation of other free bakeries, it's more of a grab and go situation. But because we were in this park, it felt like there was room to spread out and room for other activities. It became more of a community event than just a free pastry."

For people like Sara and J.R. Almanza, the event hearkens back to old Austin, a time before the tech boom when the skyline had fewer skyscrapers and when the pace of life felt slower and it was easier to strike up a conversation with strangers. After attending the free bakery once, the Almanzas decided to come back and enjoy the sense of community.

"Right now it seems like people are becoming more divided. It feels like everything's so polarizing these days," J.R. said. "There's so much out there to kind of distract us from meeting people and engaging with other people, that events like this are important because it brings people together."

That sense of community is part of what led Lanne Stauffer to create the very first Little Free Bakery in Seattle in 2021.

## **It all started in Seattle**

Stauffer got the idea for a Little Free Bakery after she experienced a small act of kindness.

"We were still in the pandemic and the mood was scared and nobody was coming out of their houses and just a lot of fear in the air and there was a bouquet of flowers on my front step," Stauffer said.

Receiving those flowers created a shift in how she was feeling inside.

"Just the joy of finding that bouquet of flowers on my front step changed my day and I wanted to know what I could do to change other folks' day in the same way," she said.

But Stauffer isn't a florist. She's a baker. She thought of Little Free Libraries and asked her husband to build her a pick-up box.

"It gives me so much joy to bake for people," she said. "It's the way I say I love you, and so even if nobody came that day, just knowing I was baking for the community made me feel good."

That Tuesday, people did come though — and in an hour all 50 little apple pies were gone. By the time it was over, Stauffer decided she would do it again the following week.

It's been five years since then, and Stauffer has noticed a couple of things. Chocolate and lemon sweets are more popular than others. And the treats aren't the only reason people stop by.

**"**People are always grateful to have a place to come and meet their neighbors and have conversations often about what's going on in the news," she said. "We stand around and hug each other or laugh or cry, share our fears, and it's just added another gathering spot in our neighborhood."

Some neighbors even plan their weeks around the pastry drops.

Erin Creighton Tozier has lived in Seattle's Magnolia neighborhood for five years, but didn't know about the Stauffer's Little Free Bakery until a year ago.

"It's just like the anchor in our week," Creighton Tozier said. "I have a demanding job, but it's like a 3 p.m. calendar marker … a break in the day to get some fresh air. Even if it's raining, no matter the weather, like my dog and I go, we have a sweet treat, we chat with our neighbors."

To celebrate her neighbors coming out for five years, Stauffer baked a 5-foot-long white cake, with orange curd filling, a cardamom cream cheese frosting and a pomegranate molasses drizzle.

Her family helped decorate it with fall fruits before they put it out in the driveway.

"I have learned that folks need to feel connected and they can feel comforted by me just baking them something," she said.

## **The growing free bakery movement**

It only took a couple months after Stauffer started the Little Free Bakery Seattle for another one to open up.

"Then it started to snowball from there, and I was having somebody reach out to me every month for a while opening a new little free bakery," Stauffer said. "I didn't know that I was starting a movement but that has been one of the biggest delights."

Now little free bakeries exist in Nashville, Tenn.; Salt Lake City, Utah; Fredericksburg, Va. and other cities.

Stauffer recently took a road trip to visit some of the other bakeries and collect stories and recipes from her fellow bakers for an upcoming book, *<u>The Little Free Bakery Book: Recipes for Sharing & Building Community,</u>* written with Jill Lightner.

Stauffer, like Mason in Austin, hopes that the movement continues to grow. "I think every neighborhood should have a little free bakery," Mason said.

In Austin, other free bakeries have popped up since Mason started hers. But the reach goes farther. In Chattanooga, Tenn., her sister plans to start a free bakery there.

"I think she just saw how much fun we're having here and thought that she wants a little slice of that in her own neighborhood," Mason said.

**"**People are always grateful to have a place to come and meet their neighbors and have conversations often about what's going on in the news," she said. "We stand around and hug each other or laugh or cry, share our fears, and it's just added another gathering spot in our neighborhood."
Some neighbors even plan their weeks around the pastry drops.
Erin Creighton Tozier has lived in Seattle's Magnolia neighborhood for five years, but didn't know about the Stauffer's Little Free Bakery until a year ago.

"It's just like the anchor in our week," Creighton Tozier said. "I have a demanding job, but it's like a 3 p.m. calendar marker … a break in the day to get some fresh air. Even if it's raining, no matter the weather, like my dog and I go, we have a sweet treat, we chat with our neighbors."
To celebrate her neighbors coming out for five years, Stauffer baked a 5-foot-long white cake, with orange curd filling, a cardamom cream cheese frosting and a pomegranate molasses drizzle.
Her family helped decorate it with fall fruits before they put it out in the driveway.
"I have learned that folks need to feel connected and they can feel comforted by me just baking them something," she said.
**The growing free bakery movement**
It only took a couple months after Stauffer started the Little Free Bakery Seattle for another one to open up.

"Then it started to snowball from there, and I was having somebody reach out to me every month for a while opening a new little free bakery," Stauffer said. "I didn't know that I was starting a movement but that has been one of the biggest delights."

Stauffer recently took a road trip to visit some of the other bakeries and collect stories and recipes from her fellow bakers for an upcoming book, *<u>The Little Free Bakery Book: Recipes for Sharing & Building Community,</u>* written with Jill Lightner.
Stauffer, like Mason in Austin, hopes that the movement continues to grow. "I think every neighborhood should have a little free bakery," Mason said.
In Austin, other free bakeries have popped up since Mason started hers. But the reach goes farther. In Chattanooga, Tenn., her sister plans to start a free bakery there.
"I think she just saw how much fun we're having here and thought that she wants a little slice of that in her own neighborhood," Mason said.

articles.title: Novel Experiments Expand the Hunt for ‘Ultralight’ Dark Matter
articles.author: Jay Bennett
articles.body_markdown:
Celsius Pictor for *Quanta Magazine*

For the most part, we are blind to the universe.

Almost a century ago — in 1933, to be exact — Fritz Zwicky’s studies of distant galaxies led him to suggest that “dark matter is present in very much greater density than luminous matter.” Observations by the astronomer Vera Rubin would later substantiate the case for the intangible, leading her to write in 1980 that “the conclusion is inescapable that non-luminous matter exists.” The elusive stuff appears to react with ordinary matter only through gravity, allowing scientists to estimate how much of it there is. Beyond that, we know very little.

That’s not for lack of trying. Elaborate detectors across the globe have failed to catch any glimpse of dark matter. If you also consider dark energy, which accelerates the expansion of the cosmos, “more than 90% of the matter-energy contents of the universe are unknown,” said Atsushi Taruya, an astrophysicist at Kyoto University in Japan. “That’s a bit embarrassing.”

As null results pile up, scientists are expanding the search, particularly for the tiniest candidates, called ultralight dark matter. Some of the more inventive experiments involve clouds of atoms in quantum superpositions, minuscule levitating magnets, nuclear atomic clocks, and Earth’s geomagnetic field itself. One of these approaches may yield a clue to a whole new realm of physics.

## **Problem Solver**

Ultralight dark matter wasn’t always a popular target. For decades, the leading candidate was a “weakly interacting massive particle,” or WIMP, but tests have steadily ruled out WIMPs with different characteristics. In September 2026, researchers working on an experiment called Lux-Zeplin said they had detected a mysterious particle collision in an underground vat of liquid xenon. The cause could have been a WIMP, but many scientists remain skeptical because the collision was so energetic — if WIMPs can have that much energy, several lower-energy collisions should have been detected already. As with other compelling apparent WIMP detections, the peculiar signal may have been a false alarm caused by rare interactions with background particles or a flaw in the data analysis.

Dennis Uitenbroek and Tjerk Oosterkamp, Leiden Institute of Physics

The September blip could end up marking one of the last gasps of the WIMP era. For years now, WIMP searches have been giving way to the hunt for lighter particles — particles so wispy that they would behave more like immense waves flowing through space.

For many scientists, the most appealing ultralight dark matter candidate is the axion. Named in the 1970s for a laundry detergent, this hypothetical particle would clean up a major problem in physics.

The problem concerns the neutron, which is made up of fundamental particles called quarks with opposing electrical charges. According to theories governing the strong nuclear force — the force that holds together atomic nuclei **—** these charges should be slightly offset. But precision measurements find them almost perfectly aligned, a mystery known as the strong CP problem. A hypothetical field of axions would pull the neutron’s internal charges into the observed alignment.

But searching for axions is a painstaking process. If they account for all or most dark matter, theories suggest that a single axion should be about a trillionth to a billionth of the mass of an electron. So far, physicists have explored only a tiny fraction of these possibilities.

One axion-hunting tool is a haloscope, a hollow device with conductive metal walls placed inside a strong magnetic field. If axions from space fly through the magnetic field inside this cavity, they should convert to photons, producing an electromagnetic signal that the experiment would amplify.

The challenge is that, for every possible axion mass, you need a different size detector. For the lighter axions, the cavity needs to have a diameter about that of a beer keg. For heavier axions, you need a smaller cavity. Haloscopes such as the Axion Dark Matter Experiment at the University of Washington have thoroughly searched much of the lighter range without finding anything.

At Yale University, the physicist Reina Maruyama and her colleagues are developing a haloscope filled with an array of copper rods that alter the experiment’s electromagnetic field. The new setup will let them search for higher-mass axions. Other possible designs split the cavity into segments, either with thin conductive walls or with honeycomb-shaped metal tubes.

These modified haloscopes should allow scientists to slowly test unexplored segments of the axion’s mass range. But to search for particles outside this range, researchers need entirely new setups.

## **Dark Worlds**

While the axion could solve the strong CP problem, it may not account for all dark matter. In fact, many physicists argue that we shouldn’t assume dark matter is just one particle. Visible matter, after all, is a particulate soup of many ingredients.

“The world that we normally interact with, it comprises all sorts of different particles,” Maruyama said. “It’s possible that … there’s a whole other world out there that is not, at the moment, visible to us.”

Some physicists believe dark matter could consist of dozens or hundreds of axionlike particles.

© DESY/Heiner Müller-Elsner

To search for them, researchers are currently upgrading a 300-meter-long apparatus in Germany known as a “light shining through a wall” experiment. The setup runs a high-powered laser through a magnetic field. The idea is to convert photons to axionlike particles, which would then pass through a barrier that blocks light. On the other side, a second magnetic field would convert the particles back to photons.

“The goal would be to open up the window to the dark sector of nature,” said Axel Lindner, a physicist who works on the experiment at the German Electron Synchrotron (DESY).

Another approach is to use Earth’s magnetic field as a detector. A group in Japan including Taruya recently analyzed 10 years of data from a magnetometer in Scotland, searching for possible axionlike particles in our planet’s ionosphere. They found 65 electromagnetic signals that match the type of signal expected from ultralight dark matter. But to conclude that a signal is from dark matter, scientists would need data from all around the globe, because Earth’s magnetic field varies at different locations.

Taruya’s team is planning to analyze additional data taken in Japan, where the signal from any axionlike particles is expected to be different. With time, perhaps scientists will be able to read the signs of dark matter in the sky.

## **Wave Riders**

Axionlike particles may reveal themselves by converting to photons in magnetic fields, but detecting other types of ultralight dark matter requires a different approach. Such particles behave like immense fields oscillating in space. With the right setup, scientists may be able to detect the ebb and flow of these dark waves.

“Theories predict that, if there is this background density, and we’re moving through it like in a spaceship, then we should be able to probe this density because it very weakly couples to quantities we can observe,” said Thorsten Schumm, a physicist at the Vienna University of Technology.

Schumm leads a team that recently developed a new type of atomic clock called a nuclear clock. Traditional atomic clocks measure the frequency of light needed to push an atom’s electrons into a higher energy state, but nuclear clocks pinpoint the frequency required to excite the nucleus itself.

©T. Schumm, TU Wien

In particular, nuclear clocks use thorium-229, an isotope of thorium in which two nuclear energy levels are nearly the same. This allows scientists to trigger the internal transition with ultraviolet lasers. It also makes the clock extremely sensitive to any outside influences on the nucleus, such as interference from a passing dark matter wave.

Already, the nuclear clock in Vienna has set new constraints on ideas that describe how ultralight dark matter could couple to photons and the strong force. “It’s really just a freak-of-nature coincidence that there are two bound states of the nucleus … \[that\] are almost exactly identical,” Schumm said.

Another tool that could pick up these dark waves is an atom interferometer. These instruments cool a cloud of atoms to nearly absolute zero, coaxing it into a wavelike state. Lasers then nudge the cloud into a superposition, meaning that its possible location gets spread out in space. When this quantum state is broken and the wavelike atoms collapse back into particles, scientists can measure the properties of their quantum wave state.

If we are immersed in the tides of dark matter, then that dark matter might introduce measurable inconsistencies into that quantum wave state — if you can make the measurements with enough precision, that is. To that end, Oliver Buchmueller, a physicist at Imperial College London, and colleagues recently demonstrated that performing this process on two clouds of atoms at once will cancel out the noise from the lasers, allowing them to search for the effects of dark matter on their atomic clouds.

“We’ve been looking for \[dark matter\] for quite some time,” Buchmueller said. “Now we have to just be open to any potential incarnations.”

Tony Luong

The recent experiment was a proof of concept that separated the two atomic clouds by just a millimeter before putting them into superposition, which is not enough to reveal the effects of dark matter. But a larger atom interferometer designed to separate clouds of atoms by about 100 meters is currently under construction at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, and another similar experiment is pending final approval at CERN. These larger instruments might just capture the undulations of dark matter waves in the next few years, when they are scheduled to begin taking data.

In theory, dark matter waves should slightly perturb everything they pass through, all the time. An international collaboration is attempting to detect these perturbations with a tiny magnet suspended in a vacuum superconducting trap. The experiment, at Leiden University in the Netherlands, is the first to search for the effects of dark matter using magnetic levitation.

“You have a levitated magnet just sitting there waiting for something to knock it around,” said Dorian Amaral, a physicist at the Institute for High Energy Physics in Spain who works on the experiment. “It’s about the size of a grain of dust.”

The speck of magnet naturally sways ever so slightly, and if that swaying is in resonance with a passing dark matter wave, the strength of the signal will become amplified, Amaral said, the way a child in a swing will soar if you push the swing at just the right moment. The team published initial findings in 2025: no dark matter spotted. But they have since upgraded the experiment to further reduce noise and levitate a larger magnet. These changes should increase the likelihood that ripples of minuscule dark matter could jostle the magnet, and they may even make it possible to detect an ultraheavy dark matter particle.

Hunting for dark matter — tuning magnetic cavities and dialing in laser frequencies, trapping clouds of atoms and combing through years of data — is slow and meticulous work. With any luck, one of these experiments will pick up a signal, registering the nearly imperceptible swell of unseen matter flowing through the universe.

Or maybe, like their predecessors, these experiments won’t find anything. If that’s the case, physicists will need to investigate other possibilities. Maybe dark matter is made up of countless primordial black holes that formed immediately after the Big Bang, an idea Stephen Hawking explored in the 1970s that has garnered fresh attention in recent years. Or perhaps we are destined to stare into space indefinitely, wondering just what it is that’s holding our universe together.

articles.title: Who is Levent Alpöge, the reclusive genius behind AI’s math conquest?
articles.author: Joseph Howlett
articles.body_markdown:
Levent Alpöge got back to the place he was crashing in New York City around 4 A.M. on November 20. He was almost done. He could almost sleep.

All that was left was to download the 17 million lines of code he’d spent the night preparing for public release. It needed to go up on his personal website, alongside a four-page statement he’d tinkered with all week. But for the moment, the code still sat on the servers of his employer, the artificial intelligence company Anthropic—which had gone public just hours earlier with the largest valuation in stock market history, making Alpöge a rich man. Once the upload was complete, he would also be one of history’s most famous mathematicians.

The code was the product of untold computing resources, months of work and decades of dreaming. It proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old math problem so formidable that it is almost beyond words; in public talks, experts have tended to simply treat it as an over-the-horizon aspiration, a “vanishing point” perspective against which all other math problems shrink. Just weeks earlier Terence Tao—arguably the world’s most famous mathematician—had declared the hypothesis out of AI’s reach (let alone that of humans) until perhaps 2050.

Now the challenge is vanquished. Alpöge’s quiet upload capped off an epochal year in which AI has systematically conquered humanity’s oldest discipline in a sequence of escalating, dramatic and controversial discoveries. And in nearly every episode of this earthshaking war for math’s soul, Alpöge has figured somehow—part battlefield champion, part horseman of the AI apocalypse, part Forrest Gump. His eccentric ways have shaped this saga, maybe more than any other single person on Earth, and thereby the course of history.

That is perhaps why people are so divided over Alpöge. “Who is this person who’s behind some of the most striking applications of AI to mathematics?” says Henry Cohn, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “This is a really interesting question that deserves a deeper answer than you can get from following him on X.”

Depending on who you ask, Alpöge is a reviled online troll—an agent of chaos laughing as his fellow mathematicians watch their intellectual landscape get carpet-bombed by his Silicon Valley cohort—or a reluctant public figure—a shy academic who has integrity and wants to forge a future where AI is mathematicians’ collaborator, not their usurper. Or maybe he’s an arrogant genius who has a chip on his shoulder and is bent on leveraging his access, his internal models and unlimited tokens, to prove his doubters wrong by snatching every remaining mathematical trophy off the shelf.

Whatever the truth is, it’s hard to know because Alpöge won’t tell. He refuses to speak to media. This article has been assembled from interviews with dozens of friends, mentors, collaborators and acquaintances.

Alpöge’s online persona is confusing and tempestuous. He topples famous conjectures with glib and gleeful social media posts—and then gets baited into emotionally replying to anonymous commenters. His X bio starts with the self-effacing descriptor “idiot” but follows with a litany of world-class accolades. There are few photographs of Alpöge online, but they all present a consistent picture: thick eyebrows over an angular, almost-elfin face, thin bangs halfway between a Beatles mop top and a bowl cut and an impish smile that reveals a slight gap between his front teeth and an unmistakable capacity for mischief.

According to numerous sources close to him, though, behind the irreverent visage is a fierce hunger for respect and recognition, paired with a boundless belief in his own capabilities—a drive shocking even to the world-class polymaths who know him. No goal is too ambitious. Even the Riemann hypothesis—math’s one true holy grail—proved to be no limit.

“He has this will to take on the world and win,” says Scott Armstrong, a mathematician at New York University and a rare Alpöge confidant. “He’s got it in spades.”

In today’s world, where large teams are the norm for any assault on frontier research problems, Alpöge is an anomaly: he mostly works alone, except, of course, for the powerful internal models he has privileged access to. “Here is a person that is larger than life,” Armstrong says. “I keep asking myself, ‘When they make the movie, who is going to play Levent?’”

Levent Alpöge was born on April Fool’s Day, 1992, along the central stretch of Long Island.

His parents, both Turkish immigrants, realized their son’s intellect was remarkable when he was just three years old. As his mother told a Turkish newspaper in 2014, she was reading him one of his favorite books and said she was too tired to continue, so Alpöge picked up where she’d stopped. At first she thought he had memorized the page, but when she gave him another book, he kept reading. Somehow, he’d learned without instruction. On the advice of professionals, they enrolled him in a nearby gifted program.

Levent Alpöge’s one sister, Elif, is a decade older, which made him practically an only child for much of the time. Alpöge was extremely athletic and especially into distance running and soccer—with his favorite soccer team being Istanbul’s Beşiktaş Gymnastics Club.

He picked up coding early. In 2009, at age 17, he connected with bioinformatics professor Xenophon Papademetris of Yale University. Papademetris’s group assigned Alpöge a research problem the team had little time for. The idea was to use Nvidia graphical processing units (GPUs)—the technology now powering the AI revolution—to recognize vascular structures in medical images.

“He helped do one of the first GPU implementations of an image analysis algorithm,” Papademetris says. “He was a 17-year-old kid who could say, ‘I will do it.’” The professor recalls what he wrote of Alpöge in his college recommendation letter, “His enthusiasm was contagious, his energy was boundless, and his confidence in his ability to overcome obstacles almost frightening.”

Alpöge’s algorithm was enough to “punch your ticket to any university in the country,” Papademetris says. “My letter was irrelevant.” As a bonus for the achievement, a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Lincoln Laboratory named an asteroid “Alpöge.”

The teenager ultimately chose Harvard University. He fell in love with math once he got there. “He distinguished himself even in that class of overachieving first-years,” says Noam Elkies of Harvard, who was his math professor that year, “finding more than half the corrections in class materials that I did not notice sooner.” Other instructors noted Alpöge’s fastidiousness could cause tensions: in a recent Bluesky post, physicist Matt Reece recalled how the young Alpöge joined Reece’s graduate physics course and so angered the students with his persistent mathematical questions that “I feared someone would actually punch him in class.”

By his junior year, Alpöge was under the tutelage of renowned mathematician Jacob Tsimerman. (A few months ago Tsimerman won a Fields Medal, math’s highest honor, and then announced he was leaving academia to work on AI safety.)

That year Alpöge participated in a well-known summer undergraduate research program at the University of Minnesota Duluth. The program’s longtime leader, Joe Gallian, recalls Alpöge as unusually buoyant and charismatic. After visiting the program, mathematician Rishi Nath said to Gallian, “Everybody wants to be like Levent.”

Alpöge did groundbreaking work that summer, publishing papers in top journals that were on par with those of established professionals. With two weeks left, Gallian gave Alpöge a particularly hard problem to occupy his remaining time. Gallan said, “Work on it until classes start, and then, if you don’t have anything, it’s fine.” But Alpöge told him, “I’ll work on it until I solve it.”

He showed similar tenacity for everything in life, Gallian says. During the Duluth group’s yearly stop at a restaurant called Betty’s Pies along Minnesota State Highway 61, three students volunteered for the “pig’s trough” challenge: if they could eat a massive pie stuffed with ice cream in 15 minutes, they’d win a free T-shirt. Alpöge did it in three minutes and 43 seconds—a record at the time.\* He also ran Duluth’s annual marathon, and Gallian snapped a photograph of him outracing everybody at an “alpine sliding” course. “You can see the competitiveness and the fierceness and the power of concentration,” Gallian says.

The following year Alpöge’s undergraduate thesis, about famous equations called “elliptic curves,” won him the illustrious Morgan Prize. In a recommendation letter, the late Harvard professor Benedict Gross called it “a tremendous piece of research for an undergraduate, at the level of an outstanding PhD thesis.” Perhaps, Gross speculated in his letter, something like a Fields Medal was in Alpöge’s future, too. Tsimerman struck a similar note in a recommendation of his own: “Often it seemed as if there was no way to proceed, and I even suggested switching problems a few times when I thought there was a dead end,” he wrote. “But Levent enjoyed the challenge too much to stop.”

Alpöge added to his illustrious CV with a Ph.D. from Princeton University and postdoctoral position back at Harvard. Bhargava also recalls a time when a family member on Long Island was ill and Levent offered to take leave from his job to move home and help. “I’ve never forgotten that gesture,” Bhargava says, calling Alpöge “a very kind and caring person.”

He joined the company under a vague title, “member of technical staff.” Anthropic declined a request to give further information about his official work. Everyone with second-hand knowledge of the arrangement, however, insists he was *not* hired to do math.

But Anthropic employees are allowed to experiment with unreleased versions of Claude in their off time. “Give a math person access to a powerful LLM \[large language model\] with access to a lot of compute,” says M.I.T. mathematician Andrew Sutherland, “and they will eventually start asking it math questions, whether you want them to or not.”

Alpöge first gained wider recognition on July 19, 2026, with a curt X post at 10:19 P.M. EDT announcing he had solved the Jacobian conjecture, one of math’s most famous problems. Another mathematician, Akhil Mathew of the University of Chicago, had thought that the conjecture might be within reach of cutting-edge AI models and had mentioned it in passing to Alpöge, who took the idea and ran with it.

This achievement was a turning point, the first really famous math problem AI solved—the sort of thing most people would’ve revealed in a long, explanatory manuscript submitted to a top math journal. To critics, Alpöge’s nonchalant post almost seemed to say, with a callous shrug, “Yup, AI is better than you now.” (Friends say Alpöge now regrets the approach he took, for which a number of prominent mathematicians have castigated him publicly and privately.)

Over the following months, Alpöge repeated this pattern again and again. He’d think of a problem, either because he knew it from his own area of number theory or because another mathematician suggested it. He’d throw his allowance of tokens and an internal version of Claude at it and then inform a few trusted outside experts of what he found. If necessary, he’d iterate based on their feedback.

These breakthroughs—too numerous and esoteric to concisely list here—spanned a breathtaking range of mathematical topics, more than any single mathematician can productively work in. Of course, Alpöge didn’t need to understand each topic completely. He would act as a kind of liaison between his legions of Claude agents and his human collaborators.

He’d give his agentic army a direction, often based on the human experts’ guidance, and they’d churn out thousands of pages of calculations, mostly in a math-slop dialect unreadable to any human. But the slop corresponded, in some impenetrable way, to actual mathematical truth. Alpöge’s task was to translate this output, with the help of yet another LLM, into readable math. He’s become a kind of LLM whisperer through this unconventional, somewhat aggravating process, which he calls “AI psychosis,” according to Ethan Sussman, a mathematician at Northwestern University.

Still, Alpöge’s correspondents all remark on his shocking ability to grasp subjects far from his expertise—and on his unflagging resolve. “I think he really does understand all this math,” Armstrong says. “He’s like some kind of genius.”

“He is exceptionally broad,” Sussman agrees. While Sussman is usually the most intense person in his collaborations, “Levent is an order of magnitude more intense than I am,” he says. Alpöge “sets his sights on the goal, and he’s like, ‘I’ll sleep when this is done.’”

In fact, the issue of Alpöge’s sleep—or lack thereof—is something many of his recent collaborators have noticed with concern. His messages and check-ins, arriving at all hours, seem untethered from any circadian routine. “I don’t know when he’s sleeping,” several of his collaborators told me.

What happened next was a crash. Just as Alpöge was nearing one of math’s loftiest summits, hoping to solve a “million-dollar” problem from the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize list—the highest-value math targets out there—Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, swooped in. Rumors had spread that Alpöge and N.Y.U. mathematician Tristan Buckmaster were about to solve the Navier-Stokes problem. Looking for a win, OpenAI’s math team threw colossal amounts of computing power at the problem over several days to get there first.

The media painted the controversy as a David versus Goliath narrative. Alpöge did his best to stay out of it and mostly avoided the uproar, while Buckmaster was cast as the human struck down by an iron-fisted tech juggernaut.

A month later OpenAI followed up the Navier-Stokes blockbuster with more than 700 additional results. The proof dump fell upon a mathematical community already in turmoil. It also scooped a number of mathematicians’ progress on important problems, including collaborations with Alpöge that were underway. Any paranoia he already felt was now magnified, and he became increasingly withdrawn, convinced that leaks between the two companies were stealing his progress.

The most impressive result in OpenAI’s dump, maybe the most impressive AI-powered result up until then, was a proof that made significant progress toward the Riemann hypothesis. This was Alpöge’s favorite problem, the one he’d harbored unspoken dreams of someday besting. Publicly, he posted on X to commend OpenAI’s team for its work. But the very same day, he started poking harder around the edges of the hypothesis with his internal version of Claude.

On October 14 Armstrong sat down on a bench in Alpöge’s hotel lobby in Aspen, Colo.

He’d messaged Alpöge, whom he knew was in Aspen for the same secret “AIxMath” conference, because he hadn’t seen him at any of the events. Alpöge said he’d been hiding out in his hotel room and suggested they go for a walk.

The two had only spoken once before, at an N.Y.U. lunch in July. Armstrong was showing Alpöge’s Jacobian conjecture X post on his phone to colleagues around the table. He couldn’t figure out why they were giggling until the stranger with a bowl cut sitting next to him turned and said with a smile, “That was me.”

They strolled through Aspen’s quiet streets for two hours, talking about the Navier-Stokes drama and the powerful, AI-fueled forces that were forging their collective future. That day Alpöge visited Princeton University, where he told Bhargava and mathematician Peter Sarnak what he’d accomplished, swearing them to secrecy and asking their advice. “It was surreal,” Sarnak says. “He was in a pretty excited state.” Alpöge spent the rest of the week holed up in Buckmaster’s N.Y.U. office, their old war room during the Navier-Stokes drama, where they now strategized the release of the Riemann proof.

Drained but exhilarated, they wrapped up their work early on Friday morning and walked to the touristy Caffe Reggio on MacDougal Street, the only place nearby that was still serving decent coffee past 2 A.M.

Love him or hate him, Alpöge has given mathematicians a human face to represent the AI revolution, to project their feelings onto as their world is turned upside down. In his statement about the Riemann proof, Alpöge gave ample praise to Claude—“Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” But he also highlighted his own agency. “It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem,” he wrote. He used a machine to beat everyone, yes, but he remains a key ingredient. The story he has spun is one of triumphant partnership, portending a bright future for math—a modern retelling of the same “lone genius” story math has always been obsessed with, updated for the AI era.

Whether he’s a visionary genius or a corporate face, his process and his foibles are a stark glimpse into math’s new, supercharged future—AI psychosis included. Riemann being solved won’t cure cancer or stop global warming. It probably won’t change your life in any noticeable way. But it marks a turning point nonetheless, one whose import will only be fully known to our future selves.

The upload finished shortly after 8 A.M. on November 20. Alpöge texted Buckmaster the link to his website and instructed him to pass it to Armstrong. “Levent and I always joked, ‘If we ever need anything leaked, we’ll just give it to Scott,’” Buckmaster says. Armstrong posted it to X immediately. It was done.

But what if there was a bug? Alpöge realized he hadn’t had time to compile the code on his own machine before uploading it. Could something have gotten garbled in the process? People around the world would download his code, and it would crash, making them doubt his claim.

It was done—the files were already online; the world already informed. But he had to know. Bleary-eyed, he started up his compiler. He could sleep once he knew he’d won.

It needed to go up on his personal website, alongside a four-page statement he’d tinkered with all week. But for the moment, the code still sat on the servers of his employer, the artificial intelligence company Anthropic—which had gone public just hours earlier with the largest valuation in stock market history, making Alpöge a rich man. Once the upload was complete, he would also be one of history’s most famous mathematicians.

And in nearly every episode of this earthshaking war for math’s soul, Alpöge has figured somehow—part battlefield champion, part horseman of the AI apocalypse, part Forrest Gump. His eccentric ways have shaped this saga, maybe more than any other single person on Earth, and thereby the course of history.

Depending on who you ask, Alpöge is a reviled online troll—an agent of chaos laughing as his fellow mathematicians watch their intellectual landscape get carpet-bombed by his Silicon Valley cohort—or a reluctant public figure—a shy academic who has integrity and wants to forge a future where AI is mathematicians’ collaborator, not their usurper. Or maybe he’s an arrogant genius who has a chip on his shoulder and is bent on leveraging his access, his internal models and unlimited tokens, to prove his doubters wrong by snatching every remaining mathematical trophy off the shelf.

Whatever the truth is, it’s hard to know because Alpöge won’t tell. He refuses to speak to media. This article has been assembled from interviews with dozens of friends, mentors, collaborators and acquaintances.

No goal is too ambitious. Even the Riemann hypothesis—math’s one true holy grail—proved to be no limit.
“He has this will to take on the world and win,” says Scott Armstrong, a mathematician at New York University and a rare Alpöge confidant. “He’s got it in spades.”

Levent Alpöge was born on April Fool’s Day, 1992, along the central stretch of Long Island.

At first she thought he had memorized the page, but when she gave him another book, he kept reading. Somehow, he’d learned without instruction. On the advice of professionals, they enrolled him in a nearby gifted program.
