That day Alpöge visited Princeton University, where he told Bhargava and mathematician Peter Sarnak what he’d accomplished, swearing them to secrecy and asking their advice. “It was surreal,” Sarnak says. “He was in a pretty excited state.” Alpöge spent the rest of the week holed up in Buckmaster’s N.Y.U. office, their old war room during the Navier-Stokes drama, where they now strategized the release of the Riemann proof.

Drained but exhilarated, they wrapped up their work early on Friday morning and walked to the touristy Caffe Reggio on MacDougal Street, the only place nearby that was still serving decent coffee past 2 A.M.

Love him or hate him, Alpöge has given mathematicians a human face to represent the AI revolution, to project their feelings onto as their world is turned upside down. In his statement about the Riemann proof, Alpöge gave ample praise to Claude—“Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” But he also highlighted his own agency. “It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem,” he wrote. He used a machine to beat everyone, yes, but he remains a key ingredient. The story he has spun is one of triumphant partnership, portending a bright future for math—a modern retelling of the same “lone genius” story math has always been obsessed with, updated for the AI era.

Whether he’s a visionary genius or a corporate face, his process and his foibles are a stark glimpse into math’s new, supercharged future—AI psychosis included. Riemann being solved won’t cure cancer or stop global warming. It probably won’t change your life in any noticeable way. But it marks a turning point nonetheless, one whose import will only be fully known to our future selves.

The upload finished shortly after 8 A.M. on November 20. Alpöge texted Buckmaster the link to his website and instructed him to pass it to Armstrong. “Levent and I always joked, ‘If we ever need anything leaked, we’ll just give it to Scott,’” Buckmaster says. Armstrong posted it to X immediately. It was done.

But what if there was a bug? Alpöge realized he hadn’t had time to compile the code on his own machine before uploading it. Could something have gotten garbled in the process? People around the world would download his code, and it would crash, making them doubt his claim.
It was done—the files were already online; the world already informed. But he had to know. Bleary-eyed, he started up his compiler. He could sleep once he knew he’d won.
\**Editor’s Note (11/25/26): This sentence was edited after posting to correct the description of Levent Alpöge’s record in the “pig’s trough” challenge.*

articles.title: The Best Books of 2026 So Far
articles.author: The New Yorker
articles.body_markdown:
Each week, our editors and critics choose the most captivating, notable, brilliant, surprising, absorbing, weird, thought-provoking, and talked-about reads. Check back every Wednesday for new fiction and nonfiction recommendations.

By The New Yorker
## Nonfiction

## Fiction & Poetry

- ### After the Flush by Nick Kawa (California)Nonfiction We may have become blithely conversant with the toilet as a consumer product, but, as the anthropologist Kawa reminds us, once the handle has been pulled or the button pressed, we tend to give no thought to the fate of our effluents. This “flush and forget” mind-set, Kawa argues, has consequences we can no longer afford to ignore. Packed with lyrical flights and an extended account of an experiment involving a toilet seat perched over a bucket, this decade-long study of sewage and waste treatment makes a compelling case for paying attention to defecation and its afterlife—even if Kawa, like so many, cannot resist the distraction of Wordle while on the can. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “What Happens After We Flush?,” by Rebecca Mead
- ### Learning by Courtney Bush (Joyland Editions)Nonfiction A buoyant, humane philosophy uplifts this debút novella, which follows a Monday in the life of Courtney, its thirtysomething narrator, as she manages a pack of four-year-olds in a private Harlem day care. “Learning” ’s characterization of these children is uncommonly complex; they are understood as neither props nor narrative addenda but, rather, as odd little people in perpetual motion, sensorily and imaginatively porous, “eating information with their entire beings.” But Bush extends a similarly generous recognition to all her characters, including the disoriented or guilt-ridden adults that swirl around the educational space. The redemptive warmth that she offers each sets her book—and her world view—apart. Buy from BookshopRead more: “The Mothers We Pay,” by Jamie Hood

*The New Yorker*.

## Last Week’s Picks

- ### Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction This genre-bending story resurrects the women who lived, toiled, and died at a Victorian psychiatric hospital in County Cork. Ní Ghríofa, an Irish poet, uses the case notes of a doctor who worked at the institution to imagine her way into the lives of the patients—women who were confined for insanity that was attributed, variously, to lactation, “overwork attending on her sick husband,” and “money troubles.” The author manages to become a “vessel, a jug of living speech,” owing to her belief that she easily “might have lived within those walls.” The resulting work is an empathetic, probing exploration of the porous contours of history, archives, and sanity itself. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### The Absent Woman by Eve Sneider (Norton)Nonfiction This poised biography of the longtime *New Yorker* staff writer Janet Malcolm brings many of the personal themes of her writing into focus. Malcolm was born in Prague in 1934, and left for New York, with her family, when she was four years old. Sneider reconstructs the most prominent turns in Malcolm’s life: a first marriage to a successful writer; her foray into psychoanalysis; the infamous legal battle that resulted from one of her reports on that subject; her enduring skepticism about journalism itself. Sneider remains conscious of the limitations of her own endeavor, quoting from Malcolm’s notes: “What people think to themselves and never write down is what their lives are about.”
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Valiant Men of War by Jonathan Lande (Yale)Nonfiction In this revealing history, Lande contends that Black soldiers enlisted in the Civil War not only to redefine the nation but to transform the South “into a home where Black men were respected, where Black families could thrive.” Black soldiers fought bravely from the conflict’s outset, aided in winning crucial battles, and ultimately occupied Southern territory, where they wielded power over former enslavers and helped “freedpeople maintain their freedom.” After the war, as white Southerners retaliated violently to reassert white supremacy, Black veterans continued working to defend the new order, adopting forms of resistance that continue today: democratic engagement through assembling, petitioning, and voting. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Stations by Louise Kennedy (Riverhead)Fiction Beginning in 1982, this potent novel spans a quarter century in the lives of a group of teen-agers from Kildare, centering on the relationship between Róisín, a bright but “actively unpopular” girl raised by a single mother, and Red, a boy from a wealthy but troubled family, who takes refuge in Róisín’s home. Eventually, they end up living in the same squat in Pimlico, where Róisín is tormented by unrequited love for Red. Kennedy excels at portraying the squalor of small-town Ireland and nineteen-eighties London, and her rendering of Róisín’s self-loathing, anguish, and emotional recklessness is tempered by the character’s dawning awareness that “there was a way to carry sadness and not destroy yourself.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

## Previous Picks

- ### The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Riverhead)Fiction In this accomplished work, both dreamlike and incisive, strange beings of an unknown nature have colonized Earth. Years after their arrival, an elderly woman with dementia, who lives in a house near a crashed Airbus A330, and her beachcomber nephew, embark on a kind of quest with no grail. The novel brings them, by turns, to a space-telecommunications facility, an abandoned museum, and other locales half prosaic, half bizarre. Flush with gorgeous descriptions of the environment and observations about art, science, difference, the past, and the future, Harrison’s book is also a reminder of how easily humanity can incorporate transformation, or dissolution: “The apocalypse seemed to withhold itself, quickly becoming just another historical continuity.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### The Intangibles by Nick Paumgarten (Penguin)Nonfiction Paumgarten’s memoir, the staff writer’s first book, traces a life in ice hockey. Elegant, funny, and moving, the book examines his various roles—a son coached by his father, a father coaching his sons, and a teammate in late-night beer-league games. The book was excerpted in the magazine. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Shakespeare at Thirty by Rory Loughnane (Princeton)Nonfiction Who was Shakespeare before he became the Shakespeare of “Hamlet” and “King Lear”? Loughnane considers the inevitability of the most celebrated English writer by concentrating on the Bard’s early life, when he was still “a relative nobody.” Alongside a nuanced picture of the poet-playwright’s upbringing, marriage, and professional beginnings, a simultaneous portrait of Elizabethan England emerges: a place of recurrent plague, political instability, bitter literary feuds, and a nascent theatregoing culture. Loughnane pays attention to the practice of collaborative playwriting, a common technique that Shakespeare moved away from as his artistry developed. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

- ### Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction The first in a planned trilogy, this richly imagined novel reanimates two historical figures: John Field, the Irish-born pianoforte prodigy and inventor of the nocturne, and Adelaide Percheron, a mixed-race woman born in French India in 1790, whom Field would marry, then discard. The novel begins with Percheron contemplating news of Field’s death, and proceeds to trace their youths, including their meeting, in 1807, when Field is humbled by Percheron’s virtuosity on the piano. The two, Li shows, might have done well to consider the opinion of a minor character: “All this talk of being a prodigy or a genius—these things often lead to misery.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### The Telephone by James Gleick (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Nonfiction A rich supply of oddities and delights peppers this history of the telephone, from an early corporate injunction on how to end calls (with the declarative “That is all”) to the range of “invisible interlopers” who have eavesdropped on our conversations since the system’s inception. Gleick, a compelling storyteller, details the battle for corporate control that followed the telephone’s multiple inventors while also attending to the many social changes that followed such a tremendous innovation. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Telephone’s Tangled History of Intimacy and Control,” by Cal Revely-Calder
- ### A World We Share by Roger Berkowitz (Yale)Nonfiction Hannah Arendt never developed a general theory of friendship, yet the concept, as this study shows, anchors much of her political thought. Combining Arendt’s written reflections with portraits of her relationships, Berkowitz offers a model of mutual understanding for our era of epidemic loneliness and polarization. For Arendt, friendship required only respect, duration, and ongoing conversation; ideological agreement wasn’t necessary, as her own friendships bore out. Her correspondence records heated debates on contentious issues, including Zionism, and it’s these encounters that give the book its force, revealing the effort needed to maintain intimacy across profound differences. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### The Channel by Jana Prikryl (Norton)Poetry “While the others spoke, my meaning was coming through.” So begins the impressive fourth poetry collection by Prikryl, who is also an executive editor of *The New York Review of Books*. A childhood spent moving between countries and languages gave her a suspicion of easy self-expression; in this volume, it inspires an extended experiment with dramatic monologue, which borrows voices like Shakespeare’s banished Cordelia to explore exile, family, and the possibilities of communicating private grief.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Trouble with Saying What You Mean,” by Langdon Hammer

- ### The Rush by Nathaniel Philbrick (Viking)Nonfiction A master chronicler of American adventure turns westward in this sprawling account of the gold rush and its aftermath, bringing three of the country’s most tumultuous decades to life with his customary storytelling brio. Though Philbrick sometimes presses his historical arguments too hard or piles on more detail than the narrative can bear, “The Rush” at its best shows how the violence and upheaval of Gold Rush California were instigated, abetted, resisted, and occasionally forestalled by marvellously specific human beings. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Gold Rush and the Making of Modern America,” by Kathryn Schulz
- From Our Pages ### To God by Esther Yi (Astra)Fiction This collection of linked stories is set in a disjointed world that is, in turns, fantastical, dystopian, metaphysical, and viscerally down-to-earth, a world that would resemble ours if we all allowed ourselves to freely question our existence and the language with which we interpret it. Both bleak and funny, the stories explore the connections and lack of connection between beings—from a nun and an amputee to boxers, construction workers, parents, children, and animals. In “Mutter,” which was published first in the magazine, a mother-daughter relationship plays out against a backdrop of endangerment; everything is at risk, from the last living California condor at the zoo to the mother’s cognitive state. “I know it’ll be hard to see me as an animal. I was your human mother for so long, after all,” the mother warns. “But understand that I’ve transformed. Understand that your human mother has gone away.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry (Transit)Fiction This poetic début novel, a finalist for the Booker Prize, is narrated largely by an unnamed curator who specializes in reconstructing scenes from the past. Her “guiding rule” is to make viewers feel as if those who would’ve inhabited her installations “have just left the room.” At the story’s outset, she begins a commission at a medieval palace, and decides to re-create a room that would have housed a particular king, whose reign has been reduced to just a single page in the historical record. Soon, the curator is transported into that king’s world, but it remains unclear whether the narrative that unfolds is a figment of her imagination. Such is the novel’s own guiding rule, to refute “the idea that we owe anyone the answers they seek—for they are theirs alone to find.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Broadway in Black & White by John MauceriJohn H. McWhorter (Norton)Nonfiction The strengths of these authors, a conductor and a linguist, combine fruitfully in this “untold story” of the Blackness of Broadway, revealing how musical innovations by Black performers and composers, sometimes embraced and sometimes resisted, shaped more familiar shows and styles. From the still minstrelsy-adjacent productions of the twenties to the improbable apotheosis of “Hamilton,” social nous and musical knowledge join to make the persuasive case that the signature sound of the American musical owes far more to Black ingenuity than most theatregoers ever realized. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Why the Broadway Musical Refuses to Die,” by Adam Gopnik
- From Our Pages ### The Bottom of the Harbor by Joseph Mitchell (Modern Library)Nonfiction This updated edition of Mitchell’s classic work of reportage, first published in 1959 and drawn from pieces the journalist wrote for *The New Yorker*, presents the writer’s portraits of New York City life alongside whimsical drawings of the places and characters he describes. Avillez, a noted illustrator, grew up in the Fulton Fish Market—“a cobblestoned stink bomb tucked under the Brooklyn Bridge,” she writes—the subject of the first piece in the book. “By drawing something you get to hold it, see its shape, decide what is important to include,” she reflects, and her delightfully playful yet exact drawings bring fresh emphasis to the keen eye with which Mitchell observed his subjects.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Ausländer by Michael Moritz (Pegasus)Nonfiction This piercing family memoir assembles a portrait of a clan that, like millions of others, was “torn to shreds by the most murderous whirlwind of the twentieth century”: the Holocaust. Moritz, a successful venture capitalist, summons up his relatives vividly. Among them is his paternal grandfather, Max Moritz, who fought for Germany in the First World War, only to be later murdered by Nazis at Dachau. Michael was born in Wales—his father, Alfred, came to England as a teen-ager, and his mother, Doris Rath, arrived on the Kindertransport—and his account is filled with both historical detail and candid observations about the gap between his and his parents’ experiences, and about his mother’s and father’s respective attitudes toward their lost homeland. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### Nobody Broke Your Heart by Jamie Fisher (Dutton)Nonfiction Fisher's intimate biography of Elliott Smith seeks to redeem our public memory of the confessional singer-songwriter who, some two and a half decades after his mysterious death, "isn't particularly well known, or well understood, but he is terribly loved." Through a magpie catalogue of unearthed lyric drafts, unheard recordings, and interviews of a hundred and forty people who knew Smith, this thoroughgoing account manages the rare achievement of music biographies: it captures Smith's presence as experienced by those who knew him, salvaging his personhood from the flattened stereotype of the tortured artist gleaned from his lyrics alone. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason (Harper)Fiction The protagonist of this engrossing novel, Sophie, begins the story freshly separated, broke, and working on the production crew of a local literary festival. Her existence is relatively isolated—she is estranged from her best friend, and confides only in her brother—until she becomes obsessed with a writer named Lilac Dunne. Sophie, along with reading Dunne’s books, listens constantly to podcasts on which she appears, and even speaks to an invented version of her, as though she were a friend. When Dunne comes to the festival and the two meet in real life, the author is icy—but also seems interested in Sophie, much to Sophie’s surprise. As their relationship develops, the roots of Sophie’s isolation are revealed—a turn that charges the novel’s argument for the value of connection, literary and personal. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

- ### Will and Attention by Meghan O'Gieblyn (Doubleday)Nonfiction “We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will.” So insists Simone Weil, the modern mystic whose ideas haunt this brave memoir. O’Gieblyn, a critic and essayist who left the church and got sober in her twenties, recounts her pandemic descent back into both temptations in a rigorous spiritual diary that wrestles with theology, philosophy, and the intoxicating appeal of relinquishing one’s will. The association of intoxication with religious ecstasy takes on a terrible force in O’Gieblyn’s account: the substance that has blighted her life also grants the surrender of self that eluded her in worship. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Is God Another Addiction?,” by James Wood
- ### Exhibit G by Fady Joudah (Milkweed Editions)Poetry “What image of childhood is enough for a people to stay alive?” Mournful questions like this one undergird Joudah’s collection, a finalist for the National Book Award, which bears witness to violence in Gaza. The book’s poems and essays are interspersed with photographs, many of children: some hauling jugs of water; some, despite their circumstances, smiling and flashing hand gestures for victory or peace. Even as Joudah examines the ways that exile, destruction, and the “white noise of genocide” warp language and the experience of time, he also condemns the tendency to fetishize hope. “A child’s smile triumphs over terror as Icarus triumphed over gravity,” he writes. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis (Norton)Nonfiction In the early months of 2025, Elon Musk, then a consultant for the Trump Administration, launched the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), with the aim of cutting two trillion dollars in federal spending. A cohort of a few dozen tech workers and entrepreneurs who “seemed to share his pleasure in the idea of people being afraid of them,” as Lewis puts it, rallied to DOGE’s cause and led a “slash and burn” assault on U.S. government institutions. In this punchy history, Lewis chronicles the experiences of a handful of public servants on the receiving end of this onslaught who refused to comply with the often illegal mandates of DOGE personnel, even at the cost of their jobs, and careers, in government. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Passengers by Alexander Maksik (Europa)Fiction Ivan, a central character in this quietly surreal novel, is determined to show his cynical twentysomething daughter, Nina, “another way of being alive.” There’s no better place to do this than Paris, Ivan has resolved, and we meet the pair in a departures terminal at LAX. Nina, with whom Ivan has a strained relationship, is quick to kick off the banter that functions as their “common language.” While they exchange insults and memories, their flight—along with all the others due to take off—becomes infinitely delayed for reasons unknown. More troubling still is that their grasp on time, then their very consciousness, begins to break down. Completely cut off from the world outside, Nina and Ivan find themselves “bound together in ways they’d not been since she was a girl.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

- From Our Pages ### In the Belly of the Whale by Ruth Margalit (Steerforth Press)Nonfiction Through ten sharply observed profiles, Margalit draws a “composite portrait” of Israel during the transformative cultural shift of the Netanyahu years. The pieces—many of them originally published in *The New Yorker*—are built on characters as vibrant, maddening, heartbreaking, and provocative as the society that they’ve helped shape. This wide-ranging survey of Israeli life invokes issues of belonging and control, perhaps best captured by a Hebrew phrase that informs Margalit’s inquiry: the question of “who the landlord is.”
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Luna, Phoenix, Queen by Julie Orringer (Knopf)Fiction At the center of this kaleidoscopic novel lies another: a handwritten manuscript about two women desperately in love. When Barr, a middle-aged writer, finds these pages hidden in his home, he quickly recognizes in the characters his wife of some thirty years, Dava, and her best friend, Svetlana. But Barr cannot confront Dava about his discovery: she’s in the throes of early-onset Alzheimer’s, trapped behind a “curtain” that “seemed to fall between her” and the world. So, instead, Barr begins transcribing Dava’s work—but transcribing turns into editing, and editing into claiming. Told in the course of four decades, and alternating between the perspectives of the couple’s colleagues and children, friends and lovers, Orringer’s novel examines justice, truth, fate, and freedom. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Yakuza by Andrew Rankin (Basic)Nonfiction The formula for Japanese gangster films is simple: crooked capitalist mobsters in pin-striped suits face off with “good yakuza,” the samurai sword-wielding gangsters who will fight, and often die, for justice. Rankin’s new history traces a cast of real life outlaws and the shifting role of the yakuza, or gangster groups in Japanese society, from their roots in samurai culture through decades of collusion with authorities during political and economic upheavals. By tracking both the ruthless modernization of criminal enterprise and the corresponding popular imagery of gangsters, Rankin illuminates the cultural impulse to invent and varnish an ideal of traditional masculinity—a romantic and morality-blurring mythology that other countries, too, might stand to examine. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Yakuza and the Way of the Would-Be Warrior,” by Ian Buruma
- ### The Decadent Movement by Laura Kolbe (Pittsburgh)Poetry This “diary in poems” documents, in reverse chronological order, the nine months of the speaker’s pregnancy and her first year of motherhood—what the book’s opening entry describes as “a span of life ranged with newish / mountains,” and pledges “not to smooth or numb.” Kolbe’s distinctive use of language brings to life this period’s wonders and difficulties, and her maximalist approach to metaphor creates many energetic images. Though visceral, musical, and tender, the collection takes a cerebral, almost scientific attitude toward maternity (the author is also a physician)—not by drawing a clinical distance but by treating it as something to be observed from every possible angle. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

- ### The Vanishing Family by Robert Kolker (Doubleday)Nonfiction Unlike Alzheimer’s, frontotemporal dementia often begins in midlife. In this searching and suspenseful chronicle, nine adult siblings reckon with the disease’s imprint on their family—their mother began to show signs of illness in her late forties—and with the question of whether to find out, through genetic testing, if they are carriers. Kolker’s granular portrait is interwoven with enlightening snippets of scientific history, but the book’s most powerful strand is about two sisters, one of whom, Sue, begins caring for the other, Christy, in her early thirties, and does so for decades. By the end, Kolker writes, their lives were “completely enmeshed, like one life lived for each other.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Days & Chances by Joanna Klink (Penguin)Poetry The carefully crafted poems in this collection explore the porousness of the boundary between inner life and external phenomena, articulating how an individual can seem grounded in space and time as a discrete being yet also be at one with the world. “Some days I am so filled with myself / I can see nothing,” one poem begins, but “Some days I’m nothing more than hearsay, / a story read back to me that makes no sense,” another muses. Klink is attuned to the ways that both nature and social environments can be suffused with memory, longing, and foreboding. Her curiosity and tenderness toward other entities, whether human, animal, or plant, is sharpened by a feeling of terminal separateness from them. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Kobuk the Destroyer by Alex Davies (Norton)Nonfiction What do AirPods, open rocket sleds, Advil bottles, and airplane black boxes have in common? In this zippy tour of a little-known industry, Davies, a journalist, catalogues the inventive, sometimes theatrical measures that test engineers take to make everyday life safer. A seemingly dry subject yields terrific anecdotes about how extreme stunts and informal daredevilry have become mainstays of safety. Davies makes the engineers’ ambition to stage reality inside a lab appear almost heroic, while reminding us that these efforts do more than keep us safe: they tell us something crucial about the prerequisites for progress. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “How Test Engineers Decide What Counts as Good Enough,” by Gideon Lewis-Kraus

- From Our Pages ### American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee (Cardinal)Fiction Lee’s epic third novel follows a Korean family of five as they move from Seoul to Sydney to Orange County, California. As they keep resettling, their social status plummets, thanks to a professional betrayal, the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and the struggle to restart life as immigrants from another continent. While the parents do whatever they can to get by, the next generation starts to ascend, in part by importing the concept of the *hagwon*, a private after-school tutoring center that preps primarily Korean-American children for success. With a light touch and a delicacy of observation and emotion, Lee takes on immigration, class, ambition, assimilation, familial loyalty, education, and more. Along the way, she examines how long and *what* it takes to build an existence and become at home in a culture that is not your own—and doesn’t want to be. An excerpt from the novel appeared first in the magazine.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### A Shadow Over the World by William I. Hitchcock (Simon & Schuster)Nonfiction F.D.R. emerges as both hero and antihero in this compelling retelling of America’s response to rising Fascism in the nineteen-twenties and the doom-laden thirties. Hitchcock, the author of several Second World War histories, recasts the U.S. government’s harrowing reluctance to intervene in a new light, asking not why the nation hesitated before addressing the threat but, rather, how, in the end, it succeeded. The book recounts the President’s “evolution from an anti-war pacifist, a nationalist, and an American exceptionalist” to the man who rallied America’s full industrial, ideological, spiritual, and military might to safeguard global democracy, and offers a new account of how antifascism became a vital part of Americans’ self-conception. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “How America Became Antifascist,” by Beverly Gage
- From Our Pages ### The Complete Stories by Ingeborg Bachmann, translated from the German by Philip BoehmTess Lewis (New Directions)Fiction This short-story collection by Bachmann, an Austrian writer of great esteem, draws together works that span her career—as well as the real and surreal. In one, which was excerpted on newyorker.com, a man’s lifelong frustration with his limp seems to come to a head. In another, a man wanders into a shop that sells dreams. The publication of this book marks the first appearance in English of many of the stories. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### Man in the Mirror by Anand Giridharadas (Knopf)Nonfiction On its face, Giridharadas’s book is an investigation of the death, in 2023, of Jordan Neely, a homeless man known for his Michael Jackson impersonations, who, on an F train, was placed in a chokehold by Daniel Penny, an ex-Marine who claimed that Neely had been threatening other passengers. But Giridharadas studies much more than that: he is interested in the city itself, and he flits between portraits of outreach workers helping the unhoused in Penn Station, government officials debating public-health policy, and the various civic tensions of a post-pandemic New York. The book was excerpted on newyorker.com. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich (Crown)Nonfiction In March, 2023, Gershkovich, a reporter for the *Wall Street Journal*, was interviewing a Russian union boss when he was blindfolded by a group of masked agents, dragged to a van, and placed in Moscow’s Lefortovo prison, under the charge of espionage. He ended up spending more than a year in the prison, and his book reveals, with a taut sense of pacing and a fastidious eye for detail, the codes and culture of life on the inside. The book was excerpted on newyorker.com.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

- ### Jean Toomer by George Hutchinson (Yale)Nonfiction This illuminating biography focusses on the Harlem Renaissance writer, best known for the experimental work “Cane,” from 1923, which has since become a highlight of modernist and African American literature. As Hutchinson makes clear, Toomer had a complex relationship to Blackness; his grandfather was the mixed-race son of an enslaved woman—a heritage that Toomer embraced, before pretending ignorance of it. He also rejected the overtly racialized way that his work was categorized, a view that sprang from his belief that all people belong to the same “basic human stock,” and that, as Hutchinson writes, “the so-called separate races were products of false labeling.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### Seasons of Fury by Rozina Ali (Crown)Nonfiction In this multifaceted portrait of Muslim life in the United States, Ali provides an intimate account of the domestic consequences of the War on Terror and the era of bigotry it launched. After 9/11, tens of thousands of ordinary Muslim citizens endured surveillance, harassment, detention, and worse. As fear metastasizes into hatred, Ali traces profound acts of personal and familial resilience amid irrevocable ruptures. What distinguishes the book, which was excerpted on newyorker.com, is how closely it documents the lives of its subjects before 9/11, too—yielding a sweeping, hundred-year-plus history of Arab and Muslim America. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf)Fiction Mandel’s latest novel is an elegant, gracefully written crime story with sci-fi shadings. It’s set in 2031, and presents two parallel time lines that comment in opposite ways on contemporary politics. In the first of these, the United States has disintegrated into warring territories, its contested zones overrun by militias. The second half unfolds in an authoritarian surveillance state—“my homeland had closed like a fist,” one character says. Mian, translated by Elettra Pauletto (Norton)Nonfiction In this travelogue of the Volga River—“Russia’s epicenter of culture, faith, and identity”—an undercover journalist grapples with contemporary Russia. Between the river’s source, entrusted to an order of Orthodox nuns, and its southern delta, where caviar bound for the Kremlin is harvested, the author journeys through a defiant country transformed by war, sanctions, and reinvigorated patriotism. Braiding snapshots of the present with history, Mian depicts a country haunted by threats to its national integrity, where people have come to believe that “questioning their leaders . . . creates social conflict and exposes the country to foreign occupation”—a tension that, he argues, has arisen in Western democracies as well. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### The Snakes That Ate Florida by Ian Frazier (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Nonfiction In this collection of essays, reported pieces, and criticism dating back to the nineteen-seventies, Frazier’s sharp eye for finding the complex in the quotidian is on full display. From tales about monster trucks and the Maraschino-cherry empire to musings about lantern flies and *Lolita*, the collection—much of which was published in this magazine—spotlights the vibrancy of topics often under-noticed. In the playful and diligent hands of the seasoned staff writer, these ordinary things feel extraordinary.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- ### Island at the Edge of the World by Mike Pitts (Mariner)Nonfiction The belief that Indigenous monuments, like those on Easter Island, must have been made by outsiders has long shaped Western accounts of such cultural achievements. In this crisp, confident, and convincing new account of the island—known to its inhabitants as Rapa Nui—and of its chroniclers, Pitts, a British archeologist, calls theories of lost European civilizations and alien drop-ins “demonstrable claptrap.” Yet, he argues, a much more reputable but equally insulting theory about Easter Island has remained influential, even dominant: the idea that the island is a cautionary tale of a people who destroyed themselves and their paradise. The story he tells—drawing on new archeological findings, a fresh reading of eighteenth-century visitors’ accounts, and a reconsideration of the archaeologist Katherine Routledge’s neglected work—is quite different, and reflects a broader shift in the consensus around Rapa Nui studies. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Easter Island and the Allure of “Lost Civilizations”,” by Margaret Talbot
- ### Jean by Madeleine Dunnigan (Norton)Fiction An English boarding school for troubled boys is the backdrop of this quiet yet accomplished début novel, set in 1976. Jean, one of the school’s teen-age charges, is the child of a single mother—a Jewish woman who was sent away from Berlin as a child, during the Second World War. Though something of an outcast, Jean finds snatches of intense companionship with another boy, with whom he has secret lakeside trysts at night, and whose fondness for Jean waxes and wanes, often depending on whether they are alone. While the novel stages Jean’s experience of being “driven uncontrollably” by desire, it also examines the weight of his and his family’s history—and the imperfect self-awareness of a young person carrying great pain. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### Hated by All the Right People by Jason Zengerle (Crooked Media Reads)Nonfiction Zengerle, a staff writer at *The New Yorker*, first met Tucker Carlson in 1997, when Zengerle was an intern at *The New Republic* and Carlson was a star reporter at *The Weekly Standard*. Carlson, who was not yet thirty, “seemed so much older, wiser, and worldlier,” Zengerle writes in his new biography. “He had a wicked sense of humor and a strong contrarian streak.” Zengerle set out to investigate—in a thoroughly reported, often hilariously told portrait—how Carlson went from a gifted young political writer to the leader of a right-wing media ecosystem that has become increasingly beholden to the viewpoints of Donald Trump. An excerpt appeared in the magazine.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

- ### One Bad Mother by Ej Dickson (Simon & Schuster)Nonfiction When being a good mother represents a structurally unattainable standard, it’s no wonder there has been a countervailing embrace of the opposite identity, that of the self-declared “bad mother.” Dickson counts herself among such mothers, listing the credentials that earn her the badge of dishonor. “I text my friends Patti LuPone TikToks while Marco is on the floor playing with his toys,” she writes. “I don’t enjoy pretend play or cooking or cleaning or birthday parties.” Dickson, who is a senior writer at *The Cut*, satirizes the good mom she fails to be and offers a brisk tour of the bad-mother trope as it now circulates in popular culture, from the question of how mothers are meant to combine parenthood with paid work to considerations of the stage mom and the MILF. Dickson writes with a refreshing absence of self-pity, and with empathy even for mothers whose practices and preferences differ vastly from her own.
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “What Makes a Good Mother?,” by Rebecca Mead
- ### Bernie for Burlington by Dan Chiasson (Knopf)Nonfiction In 1971, Bernie Sanders moved to Burlington and made his first run for the U.S. Senate, winning 2.2 per cent of the vote. That same year, blocks away from Sanders’s apartment, Dan Chiasson was born. Chiasson, a poet, a longtime contributor to this magazine, and the chair of the English department at Wellesley, had a front-row seat to Sanders’s rise, and his revelatory new book is nearly as much a memoir of its author as it is a biography of its subject and, not least, a history of the Green Mountain State. Sanders’s attraction to Vermont can be traced back to a moment when he, as a young man, came across a brochure from a Vermont travel bureau. “It is no small irony,” Chiasson writes, “that hill farms marketed to well-heeled city people piqued the interest of a thirteen-year-old Brooklyn Jew and future socialist who would arguably do more to impact Vermont’s traditional culture than anyone in the state’s history.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “When Bernie Sanders Headed for the Hills,” by Jill Lepore
- ### Everything Is Photograph by Patricia Albers (Other Press)Nonfiction This biography tracks the triumphs and the travails of the twentieth-century Hungarian photographer André Kertész. Kertész’s compositions are notably strange—often off center and taken from high angles, they appear like nervous half glances at scenes of pedestrian shuffle—and many are reproduced here, enriched by thorough commentary by Albers. Her exploration of Kertész’s time as an infantryman in the First World War is especially illuminating, as she documents the curiously “flirtatious tender touch” with which he photographed his surroundings. This kind of artistic contradiction becomes a theme, as Albers unfurls details about Kertész’s romantic life, his move to America, and his later fame. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop
- From Our Pages ### This Is Where the Serpent Lives by Daniyal Mueenuddin (Knopf)Fiction Mueenuddin’s powerfully absorbing novel charts the intricate interplay between landowners and their servants in a feudal Pakistan. Among other narratives, he traces the trajectory of one man, Bayazid—orphaned, or abandoned, as a young child in the years after Partition—who comes to accept that, though he may have left his lowly job at a tandoori stall behind, he will never rise beyond his role as a chauffeur to a wealthy family. Years later, Saqib, a similarly ambitious young man, whom Bayazid has championed, dreams of acquiring some of the riches of his employers but instead discovers that his deviously brilliant scheming could destroy him. Parts of the novel first appeared in *The New Yorker.*
Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

blocks.text: Each week, our editors and critics choose the most captivating, notable, brilliant, surprising, absorbing, weird, thought-provoking, and talked-about reads. Check back every Wednesday for new fiction and nonfiction recommendations.
By The New Yorker
Nonfiction
Fiction & Poetry

items: ### After the Flush by Nick Kawa (California)Nonfiction We may have become blithely conversant with the toilet as a consumer product, but, as the anthropologist Kawa reminds us, once the handle has been pulled or the button pressed, we tend to give no thought to the fate of our effluents. This “flush and forget” mind-set, Kawa argues, has consequences we can no longer afford to ignore. Packed with lyrical flights and an extended account of an experiment involving a toilet seat perched over a bucket, this decade-long study of sewage and waste treatment makes a compelling case for paying attention to defecation and its afterlife—even if Kawa, like so many, cannot resist the distraction of Wordle while on the can. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “What Happens After We Flush?,” by Rebecca Mead

### Learning by Courtney Bush (Joyland Editions)Nonfiction A buoyant, humane philosophy uplifts this debút novella, which follows a Monday in the life of Courtney, its thirtysomething narrator, as she manages a pack of four-year-olds in a private Harlem day care. “Learning” ’s characterization of these children is uncommonly complex; they are understood as neither props nor narrative addenda but, rather, as odd little people in perpetual motion, sensorily and imaginatively porous, “eating information with their entire beings.” But Bush extends a similarly generous recognition to all her characters, including the disoriented or guilt-ridden adults that swirl around the educational space. The redemptive warmth that she offers each sets her book—and her world view—apart. Buy from BookshopRead more: “The Mothers We Pay,” by Jamie Hood

blocks.text: *The New Yorker*.
Last Week’s Picks

items: ### Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction This genre-bending story resurrects the women who lived, toiled, and died at a Victorian psychiatric hospital in County Cork. Ní Ghríofa, an Irish poet, uses the case notes of a doctor who worked at the institution to imagine her way into the lives of the patients—women who were confined for insanity that was attributed, variously, to lactation, “overwork attending on her sick husband,” and “money troubles.” The author manages to become a “vessel, a jug of living speech,” owing to her belief that she easily “might have lived within those walls.” The resulting work is an empathetic, probing exploration of the porous contours of history, archives, and sanity itself. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Absent Woman by Eve Sneider (Norton)Nonfiction This poised biography of the longtime *New Yorker* staff writer Janet Malcolm brings many of the personal themes of her writing into focus. Malcolm was born in Prague in 1934, and left for New York, with her family, when she was four years old. Sneider reconstructs the most prominent turns in Malcolm’s life: a first marriage to a successful writer; her foray into psychoanalysis; the infamous legal battle that resulted from one of her reports on that subject; her enduring skepticism about journalism itself. Sneider remains conscious of the limitations of her own endeavor, quoting from Malcolm’s notes: “What people think to themselves and never write down is what their lives are about.”

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Valiant Men of War by Jonathan Lande (Yale)Nonfiction In this revealing history, Lande contends that Black soldiers enlisted in the Civil War not only to redefine the nation but to transform the South “into a home where Black men were respected, where Black families could thrive.” Black soldiers fought bravely from the conflict’s outset, aided in winning crucial battles, and ultimately occupied Southern territory, where they wielded power over former enslavers and helped “freedpeople maintain their freedom.” After the war, as white Southerners retaliated violently to reassert white supremacy, Black veterans continued working to defend the new order, adopting forms of resistance that continue today: democratic engagement through assembling, petitioning, and voting. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Stations by Louise Kennedy (Riverhead)Fiction Beginning in 1982, this potent novel spans a quarter century in the lives of a group of teen-agers from Kildare, centering on the relationship between Róisín, a bright but “actively unpopular” girl raised by a single mother, and Red, a boy from a wealthy but troubled family, who takes refuge in Róisín’s home. Eventually, they end up living in the same squat in Pimlico, where Róisín is tormented by unrequited love for Red. Kennedy excels at portraying the squalor of small-town Ireland and nineteen-eighties London, and her rendering of Róisín’s self-loathing, anguish, and emotional recklessness is tempered by the character’s dawning awareness that “there was a way to carry sadness and not destroy yourself.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

blocks.text: Previous Picks

items: ### The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Riverhead)Fiction In this accomplished work, both dreamlike and incisive, strange beings of an unknown nature have colonized Earth. Years after their arrival, an elderly woman with dementia, who lives in a house near a crashed Airbus A330, and her beachcomber nephew, embark on a kind of quest with no grail. The novel brings them, by turns, to a space-telecommunications facility, an abandoned museum, and other locales half prosaic, half bizarre. Flush with gorgeous descriptions of the environment and observations about art, science, difference, the past, and the future, Harrison’s book is also a reminder of how easily humanity can incorporate transformation, or dissolution: “The apocalypse seemed to withhold itself, quickly becoming just another historical continuity.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### The Intangibles by Nick Paumgarten (Penguin)Nonfiction Paumgarten’s memoir, the staff writer’s first book, traces a life in ice hockey. Elegant, funny, and moving, the book examines his various roles—a son coached by his father, a father coaching his sons, and a teammate in late-night beer-league games. The book was excerpted in the magazine. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Shakespeare at Thirty by Rory Loughnane (Princeton)Nonfiction Who was Shakespeare before he became the Shakespeare of “Hamlet” and “King Lear”? Loughnane considers the inevitability of the most celebrated English writer by concentrating on the Bard’s early life, when he was still “a relative nobody.” Alongside a nuanced picture of the poet-playwright’s upbringing, marriage, and professional beginnings, a simultaneous portrait of Elizabethan England emerges: a place of recurrent plague, political instability, bitter literary feuds, and a nascent theatregoing culture. Loughnane pays attention to the practice of collaborative playwriting, a common technique that Shakespeare moved away from as his artistry developed. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction The first in a planned trilogy, this richly imagined novel reanimates two historical figures: John Field, the Irish-born pianoforte prodigy and inventor of the nocturne, and Adelaide Percheron, a mixed-race woman born in French India in 1790, whom Field would marry, then discard. The novel begins with Percheron contemplating news of Field’s death, and proceeds to trace their youths, including their meeting, in 1807, when Field is humbled by Percheron’s virtuosity on the piano. The two, Li shows, might have done well to consider the opinion of a minor character: “All this talk of being a prodigy or a genius—these things often lead to misery.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Telephone by James Gleick (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Nonfiction A rich supply of oddities and delights peppers this history of the telephone, from an early corporate injunction on how to end calls (with the declarative “That is all”) to the range of “invisible interlopers” who have eavesdropped on our conversations since the system’s inception. Gleick, a compelling storyteller, details the battle for corporate control that followed the telephone’s multiple inventors while also attending to the many social changes that followed such a tremendous innovation. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Telephone’s Tangled History of Intimacy and Control,” by Cal Revely-Calder

### A World We Share by Roger Berkowitz (Yale)Nonfiction Hannah Arendt never developed a general theory of friendship, yet the concept, as this study shows, anchors much of her political thought. Combining Arendt’s written reflections with portraits of her relationships, Berkowitz offers a model of mutual understanding for our era of epidemic loneliness and polarization. For Arendt, friendship required only respect, duration, and ongoing conversation; ideological agreement wasn’t necessary, as her own friendships bore out. Her correspondence records heated debates on contentious issues, including Zionism, and it’s these encounters that give the book its force, revealing the effort needed to maintain intimacy across profound differences. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Channel by Jana Prikryl (Norton)Poetry “While the others spoke, my meaning was coming through.” So begins the impressive fourth poetry collection by Prikryl, who is also an executive editor of *The New York Review of Books*. A childhood spent moving between countries and languages gave her a suspicion of easy self-expression; in this volume, it inspires an extended experiment with dramatic monologue, which borrows voices like Shakespeare’s banished Cordelia to explore exile, family, and the possibilities of communicating private grief.

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Trouble with Saying What You Mean,” by Langdon Hammer

items: ### The Rush by Nathaniel Philbrick (Viking)Nonfiction A master chronicler of American adventure turns westward in this sprawling account of the gold rush and its aftermath, bringing three of the country’s most tumultuous decades to life with his customary storytelling brio. Though Philbrick sometimes presses his historical arguments too hard or piles on more detail than the narrative can bear, “The Rush” at its best shows how the violence and upheaval of Gold Rush California were instigated, abetted, resisted, and occasionally forestalled by marvellously specific human beings. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Gold Rush and the Making of Modern America,” by Kathryn Schulz

From Our Pages ### To God by Esther Yi (Astra)Fiction This collection of linked stories is set in a disjointed world that is, in turns, fantastical, dystopian, metaphysical, and viscerally down-to-earth, a world that would resemble ours if we all allowed ourselves to freely question our existence and the language with which we interpret it. Both bleak and funny, the stories explore the connections and lack of connection between beings—from a nun and an amputee to boxers, construction workers, parents, children, and animals. In “Mutter,” which was published first in the magazine, a mother-daughter relationship plays out against a backdrop of endangerment; everything is at risk, from the last living California condor at the zoo to the mother’s cognitive state. “I know it’ll be hard to see me as an animal. I was your human mother for so long, after all,” the mother warns. “But understand that I’ve transformed. Understand that your human mother has gone away.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry (Transit)Fiction This poetic début novel, a finalist for the Booker Prize, is narrated largely by an unnamed curator who specializes in reconstructing scenes from the past. Her “guiding rule” is to make viewers feel as if those who would’ve inhabited her installations “have just left the room.” At the story’s outset, she begins a commission at a medieval palace, and decides to re-create a room that would have housed a particular king, whose reign has been reduced to just a single page in the historical record. Soon, the curator is transported into that king’s world, but it remains unclear whether the narrative that unfolds is a figment of her imagination. Such is the novel’s own guiding rule, to refute “the idea that we owe anyone the answers they seek—for they are theirs alone to find.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Broadway in Black & White by John MauceriJohn H. McWhorter (Norton)Nonfiction The strengths of these authors, a conductor and a linguist, combine fruitfully in this “untold story” of the Blackness of Broadway, revealing how musical innovations by Black performers and composers, sometimes embraced and sometimes resisted, shaped more familiar shows and styles. From the still minstrelsy-adjacent productions of the twenties to the improbable apotheosis of “Hamilton,” social nous and musical knowledge join to make the persuasive case that the signature sound of the American musical owes far more to Black ingenuity than most theatregoers ever realized. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Why the Broadway Musical Refuses to Die,” by Adam Gopnik

From Our Pages ### The Bottom of the Harbor by Joseph Mitchell (Modern Library)Nonfiction This updated edition of Mitchell’s classic work of reportage, first published in 1959 and drawn from pieces the journalist wrote for *The New Yorker*, presents the writer’s portraits of New York City life alongside whimsical drawings of the places and characters he describes. Avillez, a noted illustrator, grew up in the Fulton Fish Market—“a cobblestoned stink bomb tucked under the Brooklyn Bridge,” she writes—the subject of the first piece in the book. “By drawing something you get to hold it, see its shape, decide what is important to include,” she reflects, and her delightfully playful yet exact drawings bring fresh emphasis to the keen eye with which Mitchell observed his subjects.

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Ausländer by Michael Moritz (Pegasus)Nonfiction This piercing family memoir assembles a portrait of a clan that, like millions of others, was “torn to shreds by the most murderous whirlwind of the twentieth century”: the Holocaust. Moritz, a successful venture capitalist, summons up his relatives vividly. Among them is his paternal grandfather, Max Moritz, who fought for Germany in the First World War, only to be later murdered by Nazis at Dachau. Michael was born in Wales—his father, Alfred, came to England as a teen-ager, and his mother, Doris Rath, arrived on the Kindertransport—and his account is filled with both historical detail and candid observations about the gap between his and his parents’ experiences, and about his mother’s and father’s respective attitudes toward their lost homeland. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### Nobody Broke Your Heart by Jamie Fisher (Dutton)Nonfiction Fisher's intimate biography of Elliott Smith seeks to redeem our public memory of the confessional singer-songwriter who, some two and a half decades after his mysterious death, "isn't particularly well known, or well understood, but he is terribly loved." Through a magpie catalogue of unearthed lyric drafts, unheard recordings, and interviews of a hundred and forty people who knew Smith, this thoroughgoing account manages the rare achievement of music biographies: it captures Smith's presence as experienced by those who knew him, salvaging his personhood from the flattened stereotype of the tortured artist gleaned from his lyrics alone. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason (Harper)Fiction The protagonist of this engrossing novel, Sophie, begins the story freshly separated, broke, and working on the production crew of a local literary festival. Her existence is relatively isolated—she is estranged from her best friend, and confides only in her brother—until she becomes obsessed with a writer named Lilac Dunne. Sophie, along with reading Dunne’s books, listens constantly to podcasts on which she appears, and even speaks to an invented version of her, as though she were a friend. When Dunne comes to the festival and the two meet in real life, the author is icy—but also seems interested in Sophie, much to Sophie’s surprise. As their relationship develops, the roots of Sophie’s isolation are revealed—a turn that charges the novel’s argument for the value of connection, literary and personal. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Will and Attention by Meghan O'Gieblyn (Doubleday)Nonfiction “We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will.” So insists Simone Weil, the modern mystic whose ideas haunt this brave memoir. O’Gieblyn, a critic and essayist who left the church and got sober in her twenties, recounts her pandemic descent back into both temptations in a rigorous spiritual diary that wrestles with theology, philosophy, and the intoxicating appeal of relinquishing one’s will. The association of intoxication with religious ecstasy takes on a terrible force in O’Gieblyn’s account: the substance that has blighted her life also grants the surrender of self that eluded her in worship. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Is God Another Addiction?,” by James Wood

### Exhibit G by Fady Joudah (Milkweed Editions)Poetry “What image of childhood is enough for a people to stay alive?” Mournful questions like this one undergird Joudah’s collection, a finalist for the National Book Award, which bears witness to violence in Gaza. The book’s poems and essays are interspersed with photographs, many of children: some hauling jugs of water; some, despite their circumstances, smiling and flashing hand gestures for victory or peace. Even as Joudah examines the ways that exile, destruction, and the “white noise of genocide” warp language and the experience of time, he also condemns the tendency to fetishize hope. “A child’s smile triumphs over terror as Icarus triumphed over gravity,” he writes. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis (Norton)Nonfiction In the early months of 2025, Elon Musk, then a consultant for the Trump Administration, launched the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), with the aim of cutting two trillion dollars in federal spending. A cohort of a few dozen tech workers and entrepreneurs who “seemed to share his pleasure in the idea of people being afraid of them,” as Lewis puts it, rallied to DOGE’s cause and led a “slash and burn” assault on U.S. government institutions. In this punchy history, Lewis chronicles the experiences of a handful of public servants on the receiving end of this onslaught who refused to comply with the often illegal mandates of DOGE personnel, even at the cost of their jobs, and careers, in government. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Passengers by Alexander Maksik (Europa)Fiction Ivan, a central character in this quietly surreal novel, is determined to show his cynical twentysomething daughter, Nina, “another way of being alive.” There’s no better place to do this than Paris, Ivan has resolved, and we meet the pair in a departures terminal at LAX. Nina, with whom Ivan has a strained relationship, is quick to kick off the banter that functions as their “common language.” While they exchange insults and memories, their flight—along with all the others due to take off—becomes infinitely delayed for reasons unknown. More troubling still is that their grasp on time, then their very consciousness, begins to break down. Completely cut off from the world outside, Nina and Ivan find themselves “bound together in ways they’d not been since she was a girl.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### In the Belly of the Whale by Ruth Margalit (Steerforth Press)Nonfiction Through ten sharply observed profiles, Margalit draws a “composite portrait” of Israel during the transformative cultural shift of the Netanyahu years. The pieces—many of them originally published in *The New Yorker*—are built on characters as vibrant, maddening, heartbreaking, and provocative as the society that they’ve helped shape. This wide-ranging survey of Israeli life invokes issues of belonging and control, perhaps best captured by a Hebrew phrase that informs Margalit’s inquiry: the question of “who the landlord is.”

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Luna, Phoenix, Queen by Julie Orringer (Knopf)Fiction At the center of this kaleidoscopic novel lies another: a handwritten manuscript about two women desperately in love. When Barr, a middle-aged writer, finds these pages hidden in his home, he quickly recognizes in the characters his wife of some thirty years, Dava, and her best friend, Svetlana. But Barr cannot confront Dava about his discovery: she’s in the throes of early-onset Alzheimer’s, trapped behind a “curtain” that “seemed to fall between her” and the world. So, instead, Barr begins transcribing Dava’s work—but transcribing turns into editing, and editing into claiming. Told in the course of four decades, and alternating between the perspectives of the couple’s colleagues and children, friends and lovers, Orringer’s novel examines justice, truth, fate, and freedom. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Yakuza by Andrew Rankin (Basic)Nonfiction The formula for Japanese gangster films is simple: crooked capitalist mobsters in pin-striped suits face off with “good yakuza,” the samurai sword-wielding gangsters who will fight, and often die, for justice. Rankin’s new history traces a cast of real life outlaws and the shifting role of the yakuza, or gangster groups in Japanese society, from their roots in samurai culture through decades of collusion with authorities during political and economic upheavals. By tracking both the ruthless modernization of criminal enterprise and the corresponding popular imagery of gangsters, Rankin illuminates the cultural impulse to invent and varnish an ideal of traditional masculinity—a romantic and morality-blurring mythology that other countries, too, might stand to examine. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Yakuza and the Way of the Would-Be Warrior,” by Ian Buruma

### The Decadent Movement by Laura Kolbe (Pittsburgh)Poetry This “diary in poems” documents, in reverse chronological order, the nine months of the speaker’s pregnancy and her first year of motherhood—what the book’s opening entry describes as “a span of life ranged with newish / mountains,” and pledges “not to smooth or numb.” Kolbe’s distinctive use of language brings to life this period’s wonders and difficulties, and her maximalist approach to metaphor creates many energetic images. Though visceral, musical, and tender, the collection takes a cerebral, almost scientific attitude toward maternity (the author is also a physician)—not by drawing a clinical distance but by treating it as something to be observed from every possible angle. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Vanishing Family by Robert Kolker (Doubleday)Nonfiction Unlike Alzheimer’s, frontotemporal dementia often begins in midlife. In this searching and suspenseful chronicle, nine adult siblings reckon with the disease’s imprint on their family—their mother began to show signs of illness in her late forties—and with the question of whether to find out, through genetic testing, if they are carriers. Kolker’s granular portrait is interwoven with enlightening snippets of scientific history, but the book’s most powerful strand is about two sisters, one of whom, Sue, begins caring for the other, Christy, in her early thirties, and does so for decades. By the end, Kolker writes, their lives were “completely enmeshed, like one life lived for each other.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Days & Chances by Joanna Klink (Penguin)Poetry The carefully crafted poems in this collection explore the porousness of the boundary between inner life and external phenomena, articulating how an individual can seem grounded in space and time as a discrete being yet also be at one with the world. “Some days I am so filled with myself / I can see nothing,” one poem begins, but “Some days I’m nothing more than hearsay, / a story read back to me that makes no sense,” another muses. Klink is attuned to the ways that both nature and social environments can be suffused with memory, longing, and foreboding. Her curiosity and tenderness toward other entities, whether human, animal, or plant, is sharpened by a feeling of terminal separateness from them. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Kobuk the Destroyer by Alex Davies (Norton)Nonfiction What do AirPods, open rocket sleds, Advil bottles, and airplane black boxes have in common? In this zippy tour of a little-known industry, Davies, a journalist, catalogues the inventive, sometimes theatrical measures that test engineers take to make everyday life safer. A seemingly dry subject yields terrific anecdotes about how extreme stunts and informal daredevilry have become mainstays of safety. Davies makes the engineers’ ambition to stage reality inside a lab appear almost heroic, while reminding us that these efforts do more than keep us safe: they tell us something crucial about the prerequisites for progress. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “How Test Engineers Decide What Counts as Good Enough,” by Gideon Lewis-Kraus

From Our Pages ### American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee (Cardinal)Fiction Lee’s epic third novel follows a Korean family of five as they move from Seoul to Sydney to Orange County, California. As they keep resettling, their social status plummets, thanks to a professional betrayal, the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and the struggle to restart life as immigrants from another continent. While the parents do whatever they can to get by, the next generation starts to ascend, in part by importing the concept of the *hagwon*, a private after-school tutoring center that preps primarily Korean-American children for success. With a light touch and a delicacy of observation and emotion, Lee takes on immigration, class, ambition, assimilation, familial loyalty, education, and more. Along the way, she examines how long and *what* it takes to build an existence and become at home in a culture that is not your own—and doesn’t want to be. An excerpt from the novel appeared first in the magazine.
