items: ### A Shadow Over the World by William I. Hitchcock (Simon & Schuster)Nonfiction F.D.R. emerges as both hero and antihero in this compelling retelling of America’s response to rising Fascism in the nineteen-twenties and the doom-laden thirties. Hitchcock, the author of several Second World War histories, recasts the U.S. government’s harrowing reluctance to intervene in a new light, asking not why the nation hesitated before addressing the threat but, rather, how, in the end, it succeeded. The book recounts the President’s “evolution from an anti-war pacifist, a nationalist, and an American exceptionalist” to the man who rallied America’s full industrial, ideological, spiritual, and military might to safeguard global democracy, and offers a new account of how antifascism became a vital part of Americans’ self-conception. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “How America Became Antifascist,” by Beverly Gage

From Our Pages ### The Complete Stories by Ingeborg Bachmann, translated from the German by Philip BoehmTess Lewis (New Directions)Fiction This short-story collection by Bachmann, an Austrian writer of great esteem, draws together works that span her career—as well as the real and surreal. In one, which was excerpted on newyorker.com, a man’s lifelong frustration with his limp seems to come to a head. In another, a man wanders into a shop that sells dreams. The publication of this book marks the first appearance in English of many of the stories. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### Man in the Mirror by Anand Giridharadas (Knopf)Nonfiction On its face, Giridharadas’s book is an investigation of the death, in 2023, of Jordan Neely, a homeless man known for his Michael Jackson impersonations, who, on an F train, was placed in a chokehold by Daniel Penny, an ex-Marine who claimed that Neely had been threatening other passengers. But Giridharadas studies much more than that: he is interested in the city itself, and he flits between portraits of outreach workers helping the unhoused in Penn Station, government officials debating public-health policy, and the various civic tensions of a post-pandemic New York. The book was excerpted on newyorker.com. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich (Crown)Nonfiction In March, 2023, Gershkovich, a reporter for the *Wall Street Journal*, was interviewing a Russian union boss when he was blindfolded by a group of masked agents, dragged to a van, and placed in Moscow’s Lefortovo prison, under the charge of espionage. He ended up spending more than a year in the prison, and his book reveals, with a taut sense of pacing and a fastidious eye for detail, the codes and culture of life on the inside. The book was excerpted on newyorker.com.

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Jean Toomer by George Hutchinson (Yale)Nonfiction This illuminating biography focusses on the Harlem Renaissance writer, best known for the experimental work “Cane,” from 1923, which has since become a highlight of modernist and African American literature. As Hutchinson makes clear, Toomer had a complex relationship to Blackness; his grandfather was the mixed-race son of an enslaved woman—a heritage that Toomer embraced, before pretending ignorance of it. He also rejected the overtly racialized way that his work was categorized, a view that sprang from his belief that all people belong to the same “basic human stock,” and that, as Hutchinson writes, “the so-called separate races were products of false labeling.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### Seasons of Fury by Rozina Ali (Crown)Nonfiction In this multifaceted portrait of Muslim life in the United States, Ali provides an intimate account of the domestic consequences of the War on Terror and the era of bigotry it launched. After 9/11, tens of thousands of ordinary Muslim citizens endured surveillance, harassment, detention, and worse. As fear metastasizes into hatred, Ali traces profound acts of personal and familial resilience amid irrevocable ruptures. What distinguishes the book, which was excerpted on newyorker.com, is how closely it documents the lives of its subjects before 9/11, too—yielding a sweeping, hundred-year-plus history of Arab and Muslim America. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Exit Party by Emily St. John Mandel (Knopf)Fiction Mandel’s latest novel is an elegant, gracefully written crime story with sci-fi shadings. It’s set in 2031, and presents two parallel time lines that comment in opposite ways on contemporary politics. In the first of these, the United States has disintegrated into warring territories, its contested zones overrun by militias. The second half unfolds in an authoritarian surveillance state—“my homeland had closed like a fist,” one character says. Mandel’s characters are attuned to beauty, in nature and in fine art, and her sentences share this aesthetic orientation. She repeats evocative images—a character swan-diving into water, for example—investing them with cumulative meaning. This piling, as much as her propulsive, suspenseful plot, supports the book’s slow-burning sense of revelation. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Emily St. John Mandel’s Fluid New Novel,” by Katy Waldman

### That Summer’s End by Lee Seong-bok, translated from the Korean by Anton Hur (Knopf)Poetry Nature, loss, and longing inspire these quiet verses, which conjure a sense of the immense mysteries governing the observable world. “How do feelings come / a bough first blossoms,” the book’s opening poem, “Feeling,” begins. “Is that how feelings come / a bough first drops its blossoms / Is that how feelings fall.” Lee’s lines have the intimacy and metaphysical heft of prayer; their elegant recursions and repetitions call to mind the cycles of life, death, and rebirth. Many of his poems are titled simply, in reference to the people, objects, animals, and abstractions on which he trains his attention—“Sea,” “Mountain,” “Cat,” “Child.” Throughout, Lee’s invocations imbue his subjects with an air of divinity. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Everywhere Millionaire by Owen ZidarEric Zwick (Henry Holt)Nonfiction This brilliant new book identifies something close to a new class in America: the ordinary, ubiquitous business owners—car dealers, beer-distribution magnates, medical-practice partners—that, for all the fuss around billionaires, collectively represent today’s “real rich.” Drawing on years of investigating how much tax business owners pay, these two economists attribute the secret ingredient of the everywhere millionaires’ success not to dazzling innovation, but rather, to remorselessness, ingenuity, and resilience. The dark side of their savvy: a history of lobbying for restrictive practices designed to prevent new entrepreneurs from getting rich in the same ways. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Wealthiest—and Stealthiest—Class in America,” by John Lanchester

### Dèy by Edwidge Danticat (Knopf)Fiction Set among Haitian Americans in Miami, this novel centers on Magnolia, a young mother who is at a mall when a mass shooter opens fire. She escapes and, because she does not want to be defined by the tragedy, decides not to tell anyone about it. In the weeks that follow, Magnolia plans her daughter’s birthday, negotiates her relationship with her daughter’s father, and coördinates medical care for her aging parents, who are living in Haiti amid growing violence. This fascinatingly banal aftermath forces the reader to confront the normalcy of such horror in a world where approximately seven per cent of American adults have been at the scene of a mass shooting. Danticat asks, Is gun violence newsworthy anymore? Or is it everyday life? Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Etna by Paul Yoon (Scribner)Fiction This novel’s narrator is a dog who lives on a farm in a nameless country that is descending into war. One day, a woman arrives who can speak with him telepathically; she names him Etna and takes him to be trained by American soldiers as a combat dog. After years of conflict, Etna is a grizzled veteran who knows how to search for explosives and how to kill. But, when the war ends, the world as he knew it has been destroyed. He abandons his handlers and wanders the wasted land, searching for any home that might be left. Yoon’s choice to plant his sparely written novel in a canine perspective reveals the devastation that human aggression can inflict on all creatures. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### Switzy by Emma Cline (Random House)Fiction Cline, as she said in a Q. and A. for this magazine, is “always interested in consciousness, and how to render our experience as humans on the page.” The human whose experience she renders in her third novel is a retired businessman who, grappling with the onset of dementia, has decided to end his life voluntarily, in Switzerland, while he’s still able to make the decision to do so. His trip to Zurich is, in a sense, a journey of atonement, with stops along the way to say goodbye or attempt to make amends. Guilty of the smaller crimes of life—he has been unkind at times, oblivious of the needs of loved ones, cruel to friends—he is, ironically, blessed with a clearer vision of himself, just as much of his mind fogs over. A painful, often darkly funny reckoning, “Switzy” was excerpted in the magazine. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Unbelonging by Catherine Jagoe (Wisconsin)Nonfiction This sensitively observed essay collection, by a translator of Spanish literature, considers the elusive nature of home. “Defining home, identifying a homeland, feeling at home. I just can’t seem to manage it,” Jagoe writes. In trying, however, she ranges elegantly across experiences, from the ecstasy of swimming to the “deep, dark wintering” of depression. The act of patiently noticing the physical world runs through the book. In Madrid, she reëncounters the “upland light, landscape, and air” of Nigeria, where she lived as a small child; and though southern Wisconsin, where she lives today, lacks the “transparent, haunting fragrance” of wild bluebells in the woods of England, her country of birth, she discovers a place for herself there nonetheless, through close engagement with the landscape. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Israel: What Went Wrong? by Omer Bartov (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Nonfiction Gaza’s ruin, the apartheid in the West Bank, and the ascendancy of Israel’s far right can, Bartov argues, be traced to a principal failure of pre-state Zionism: neglecting to reckon with the Arabs already living in Palestine. A Holocaust historian and former I.D.F. soldier, Bartov offers an urgent and important critique of the country’s increasingly extreme religious nationalism, while reminding readers that “this was a long process and never an inevitable one.” Any hope for change, he concludes, will involve pressure from the rest of the world. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Is Zionism’s Moral Crisis About Roads Not Taken—or Original Sin?,” by Isaac Chotiner

### All Them Dogs by Djamel White (Riverhead)Fiction “I was Wardy. Tony bleeding Ward. Lethal weapon forged in 1997,” the protagonist of this bold début novel proclaims. The statement is mainly a reminder to himself, as he returns home to Dublin after five long years on the run. Tony had to flee after killing a member of a rival gang; now he has joined the ranks of another outfit, notionally in search of money and protection, but ultimately out of a longing to have “someone else do the thinking.” As Tony strains to navigate brewing street wars, the most intimidating battles he faces are still internal—between expectation and desire, between who he is and who he might want to be. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### American Sophistication by Ross Posnock (Princeton)Nonfiction “This is how the ‘sophisticated’ talk about sophistication: they don’t.” So begins this new study of the American sense of “cool,” before then embarking on an encyclopedic review of the ideal from pre-Revolutionary times to the postmodern age. Breathtakingly large in scope and purpose, and almost flamboyantly digressive and parenthetical, it’s sure to entertain and provoke. Ultimately, Posnock argues the high-water mark of American sophistication was in the nineteen-fifties, and offers a grand unified theory of the subject—one that identifies a particularly American spin on older European ideals and uncovers the values baked into its casual style. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Art of American Sophistication,” by Adam Gopnik

### Sex and Dissent by Meaghan Beatley (Penguin)Nonfiction This vividly reported book centers on recent feminist movements in Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Spain. Beatley, a journalist, profiles women protesting abortion restrictions, sexual assault, and femicide—an act that, she writes, lies “atop layers of normalized and socially sanctioned abuse.” While documenting acts of resistance, she examines the way that these feminists’ cultural contexts inflect their organizing. As she points out, many were influenced by struggles against military dictatorships of the twentieth century; some are the children of disappeared dissidents. “What sets Latin America apart is not violence itself but the clarity with which women understand its roots,” she writes. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Disappearers by Marlon James (Riverhead)Fiction This novel, James’s sixth, follows a group of gay men in Jamaica who seek love, connection, and restitution after a bloody homophobic attack. The explosion of malice effaces the men in different ways, and the book traces the mechanisms of their vanishing, examining how a person’s life can be compressed into smaller and smaller spaces. James blurs his actors together in slightly eerie ways, as if to show how suffering flattens and homogenizes its victims. But the permeability of James’s protagonists also suggests the liberating malleability of social roles. “The Disappearers” uses the tricks of fiction to pull off something extremely difficult: giving full weight to tragedy and injustice without implying that some lives are over before they’ve begun. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “ ‘The Disappearers’ Stages the Pain and Pleasure of Jamaican Gay Life,” by Katy Waldman

### Solstice by Carol Gilligan (Random House)Fiction This tender novel of intimacy and its risks begins in Boston in 1969, as Eve, a dancer, commences an affair with a colleague—an indiscretion that spurs her husband, a journalist named Gabe, to cheat, too. Under the influence of their era’s changing sexual mores, they soon reconcile. But then, in the eighties, Gabe returns from a reporting trip to the Middle East having taken up with a much younger woman. By this time, the couple share decades of history, along with three children. Gilligan’s portrait of their relationship is a study of how time binds people together. “There was a membrane now stretching between them,” she writes, “encompassing the two of them and enclosing them, fragile and yet impermeable.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Endless Endings by Ricard Solé, translated from the Spanish by Eduardo Aparicio (Princeton)Nonfiction A single cell serves as the starting point for this lyrical exploration of death. From a consideration of apoptosis—the orderly elimination of damaged or unnecessary cells—Solé moves on to failing machines, eroded memories, vanished languages, brittle digital archives, and more. His overarching idea is that organisms, minds, technologies, and cultures survive by sustaining flows of matter, energy, or information; their final deaths occur not when a single constituent part disappears but when the processes holding the larger system together falter. Solé reveals a paradox: death is not merely life’s opposite but also one of its organizing forces, a constant cycle of removal and renewal through which complex systems are preserved. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Black Shield by Wilbert L. Cooper (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Nonfiction In this multilayered work, a journalist examines a Black police organization, known as the Black Shield, that emerged in Cleveland in the nineteen-forties, alongside his own parents’ membership in it. Cooper assesses the notion that Black communities are “safer and served better” when the police who surveil and discipline them are Black, too. In theory, he writes, the Black Shield offers opportunity for young people living in the economically distressed community where it is based, but he concludes that the group is less focussed on justice than on “getting the same lack of accountability that White officers enjoyed.” His ultimate indictment is nuanced, and has shades of appreciation—for his parents, and for the badge that “shielded my family.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Supremacy by Nikolas BowieDaphna Renan (Norton)Nonfiction This formidable, sharply argued history of the Supreme Court tracks the ascendance of “judicial supremacy” over two hundred years, focussing on how the Court seized the power to strike down acts of Congress. Its power to invalidate state and local laws is a double-edged sword, but its ability to overrule a coequal branch, the authors maintain, has reliably served regressive ends. By tracing the origins of this self-conferred authority, the Harvard Law School professors make the provocative case that the Supreme Court needs to be cut down to size, and that Congress should reclaim its rightful authority. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Has the Supreme Court Sandbagged Democracy?,” by Daniel Immerwahr

### I Was Bonnie & Clyde by Laura Kasischke (Copper Canyon)Poetry The wily, beguiling poems in this collection probe selves and stories as sites of rupture and refraction. The book’s eponymous poem, for instance, begins, “You were Friday & Death. / I was Jekyll & Hyde. / You were my mother. / I Alive.” Throughout, Kasischke’s images ricochet off one another—suggesting narrative while resisting its confines, evoking stereotypical ideas and expectations of Western womanhood only to upend them. In a voice at once biting and contemplative, eerie and funny, Kasischke crafts poems in which nothing is ever stable or resolved. There is only “The confusion of the past / as fireproof as ash. // The follies of the future / as bulletproof as water.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State by Jill Lepore (Liveright)Nonfiction In this wide-ranging history, Lepore traces the ideas and technologies that have transformed political life, from census-taking and technocracy to social media and A.I. Our growing reliance on machines to predict and shape human behavior, Lepore argues, threatens democratic self-government and augurs a deeper estrangement from the natural world. The book grew out of a piece that ran in the magazine in 2024. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### The Anniversary by Andrea Bajani, translated from the Italian by Geoffrey Brock (Other Press)Fiction “Ten years ago, I saw my parents for the last time,” proclaims the narrator—an unnamed man—of this unsparing novel. “I’ve erected an impregnable wall and put an ocean between us. They’ve been the best ten years of my life.” He, in commemoration of the decade-long estrangement from his mother and father, reflects on their lives and on his upbringing. The book, which was excerpted in the magazine, challenges readers to reconsider what they owe their families, particularly in light of what they owe themselves. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### A Tender Age by Chang-rae Lee (Riverhead)Fiction In the spring of 1976, Jeon-Gi, the narrator of Lee’s seventh novel, is on the cusp of turning eleven. He’s growing up at a time when childhood is a free-range affair, and he spends hours roaming outside with a gang of other kids, figuring out how to negotiate both a fractured friendship and the demands of a neighborhood bully. His parents, recent Korean immigrants, know little of his troubles, and are shocked when violence erupts and fifth grade for Jeon-Gi comes to an abrupt halt. A summer camp, organized by a Korean church, gives him an opportunity to forge new friendships, but, once again, everything changes in an instant. Years later, Jeon-Gi is still haunted by his actions—and the lingering mystery of his intentions. In this immersive and thought-provoking novel, which was excerpted in the magazine, the reader may feel more sympathy for Jeon-Gi than he does for himself. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Yahoo Boys by Carlos Barragán (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Nonfiction In 2022, the author of this engrossing investigation travelled to Lagos, Nigeria, to find the person who, years earlier, ensnared his mother in an online romance scam. What he discovered was a place primed by its history and its poverty for the emergence of youths, known as Yahoo Boys, dedicated to conning Western marks using false identities, fake naked pictures, and flattery. In Barragán’s account, Nigerian public discourse casts the Yahoo life style—fuelled by drugs and extravagant spending—as a double-edged sword, both a stain on the country’s reputation and a powerful economic engine. As the book follows four Yahoos, it assembles a story of loneliness in the digital age—a loneliness that deforms scammer and scammed alike. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### A Scandal in Königsberg by Christopher Clark (Penguin Press)Nonfiction This fine and detailed book reconstructs a sex scandal that erupted in the eighteen-thirties in the Prussian city of Königsberg, which quickly captured public attention across the kingdom and beyond. After an earnest clergyman, with long shiny curls parted “like a lady,” attracted a cluster of devoted women followers, it didn’t take long for townspeople to suspect the charismatic cleric of arousing more than religious zealotry. Clark highlights the now familiar patterns of public inquisition from this odd historical case study, with rumors elevated into accusations and lives destroyed before anyone has established what has actually happened. As the book’s foreword cautions: “Resemblances to present-day persons and situations, though not intended, cannot be ruled out.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Anatomy of a Sex Scandal,” by Adam Gopnik

### Unsayable by Michael Cunningham (Random House)Nonfiction When this warm memoir begins, the author, a celebrated novelist, observes that the world is “sufficient unto itself. It neither knows nor cares if anyone writes about it.” Why write, then? In the pages that follow, Cunningham remembers his upbringing in middle-class suburban California, his gradual awareness of his gayness, his time as a countercultural student at Stanford, and his stints working as a hustler and a bartender, all the while elaborating writing’s many purposes—and offering guidance on how to do it well. It’s a way to entertain, to turn “ephemera into objects,” to “render and recognize everything and everyone.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### A Violent Masterpiece by Jordan Harper (Mulholland)Fiction Harper’s crime novel alternates between the perspectives of three characters. Kara Delgado works as a fixer at L.A.’s premier concierge service, catering to the outré tastes and perversions of the city’s élite. Doug Gibson is a pugilistic criminal-defense lawyer, the kind with ads on bus-stop benches. Jake Deal, formerly employed to dig up secrets for a gossip website, now works for himself as a live-streamer; he drives through the city, using a police scanner to track down scenes of chaos and carnage, feeding his viewers’ appetite for vérité gore. What is the line, Harper seems to ask, between documenting the horrors of the world and profiting from them, packaging them for an audience safe at home? Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Presence by Erin Maglaque (Astra)Nonfiction This “hidden history of the female body” reveals the ways that natural processes, such as giving birth, have been shaped by changing medical beliefs and social arrangements. Drawing on physicians’ casebooks, midwifery manuals, household recipe collections, court testimonies, private letters, and more, Maglaque constructs a kind of organic catalogue raisonné, indexing women’s experiences of their bodies from the fifteen-hundreds to the eighteen-hundreds. Her account is assembled from sharp examples. The “supposedly simple and natural gesture” of breast-feeding, for instance, came to be ruled by a “coarse moralism” in the eighteenth century, when the act “became the primary scene of sentimental motherhood: done out of a strictly defined maternal love” rather than as paid work. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson (Pamela Dorman)Fiction At the outset of this chatty novel, the protagonist, Caroline, who was recently ghosted by a thoughtless man, has had a story published in this magazine. In an uncharacteristically impulsive move, she decides to quit her job and write full time. Because her mother is a successful writer—and likely a narcissist—the decision is a complicated one. But soon Caroline finds herself at a seaside residency in Massachusetts, where she falls in love with a local. As she gets to know his childhood friends, whom Jackson renders vividly, further complications mount; one of the group, it emerges, is pregnant with his child. The novel is ultimately a study of the season in life when friendships are tested by growing families and by the realization of ambition. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness by Cal Flyn (Viking)Nonfiction What does it mean for something to be considered “wilderness” in a world saturated by human intervention? Searching for answers, Flyn travels to various remote sites—including the Transylvanian Alps; the Niassa Special Reserve, in Mozambique; and the Southern Ocean, near Antarctica—journeys that lead her to conclude that wilderness is “a negative definition, an absence.” For one thing, wild places are increasingly threatened by the trophy-hunting industry, scientific study, and corporate exploitation. But, for another, Flyn argues, wilderness is about being able to “open oneself to the immensity of all existence, all creation, all of everything.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### The Ego Trip by Kimon de Greef (Doubleday)Nonfiction De Greef’s true-crime thriller, which grew from reporting originally published in *The New Yorker*, explores the origins of the toad-smoking movement, and the trail of death and abuse that one psychedelic guru left in his wake.

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Queen Mab by Emily McBride (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction Madeleine is a “*promising*” twenty-three-year-old graduate student who decides, to the shock of other academic women in her life, to have a baby. (“They all say congrats, by the way, and better you than them,” one colleague says.) The body horror of birth gives way to the fairy-tale horror of early motherhood, which McBride, a translator based in Barcelona, strews with literary Easter eggs from folktales and Victorian poetry. Is the baby really a baby, or has it been replaced by a changeling? Is Madeleine still herself, or has she been stolen away, too? Can her husband be trusted? The result is an agile, unsettling novel about the unwinding of a mind, set in a world of women who view motherhood as a curious affectation.

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Daylight Come by Joshua Jelly-Schapiro (Penguin Press)Nonfiction This biography of Harry Belafonte, who died in 2023, paints the singer and civil-rights activist as “our first post-racial pop star.” In his music, Belafonte sought to honor his Caribbean heritage—he was born in Harlem to Jamaican parents in 1927—without being reduced to a mere exotic persona. Throughout his career, he merged his work as an entertainer with his political convictions (he refused to perform in segregated venues, for instance), a pursuit that required him to square his fame “with his anger at the society that gave it to him.” Jelly-Schapiro draws on a range of sources, including conversations with Belafonte, presenting a portrait of a formidable figure who, as Belafonte’s son puts it, “was serving two families: us and the family of Man.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### We Were Forbidden by Jacqueline Harpman, translated from the French by Ros Schwartz (Transit)Fiction In “The Ardennes Forest,” one of the three newly translated stories in “We Were Forbidden,” male and female soldiers rove aimlessly through the woods, unsure whether they’re still at war. The story’s dreamlike, surreal style permits few identifying markers; we never find out what conflict the characters have stumbled into, only that they await the activation of their “post-hypnotic orders.” “The Outcast” similarly circles feelings of entrapment, disorientation, and exile: its narrator is unkind to a hypocritical classmate at her French school in Morocco, and her teachers punish her with forty days of “ostracization,” during which no one speaks to her and she doesn’t speak to anyone. The gem of the collection is its longest story, “The Broom Closet,” an arch, light-fingered, and very funny exploration of the relationship between fantasy and fiction-making. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “An Uncompromising Belgian Novelist’s Afterlife as a BookTok Star,” by Katy Waldman

### Dooneen by Keith Ridgway (New Directions)Fiction This strange, ambitious novel is set in a version of Dublin where cars have been banned and people enter the country by teleportation. Bartholomew Port, an Irish writer living in London, returns to his homeland to participate in a literary festival, and arrives on the eve of a populist uprising. Dublin, he observes, has become a machine “for enriching the rich” and “impoverishing the poor,” a place where “life is not as important as money.” As Port falls in with a group of conspirators preparing for the insurrection, the book takes on a hallucinatory, digressive quality, blurring the lines between life and death, reality and illusion. Ultimately, Ridgway asks what responsibility bystanders must take for the injustices around them. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Frenchmen by Emily Eakin (Penguin Press)Nonfiction This stylish group biography of eight structuralist and post-structuralist philosophers interweaves details of its subjects’ lives with careful close readings and memoir. Eakin, an editor at the *Times Book Review*, aims to “re-embody” the so-called French theorists, “to recover the hidden human element beneath their often stringent antihumanism.” Her biographical approach allows her to highlight connections that a more straightforward intellectual history might not, such as the role that a chance encounter between the linguist Roman Jakobson and the anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss played in the development of the latter’s thought.

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “The Men Who Made Theory French,” by Dayna Tortorici

items: From Our Pages ### Beginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli (Knopf)Fiction After an “entangled divorce,” a woman escapes with her daughter to Catania, a port city on Sicily’s eastern coast. Upon arrival, they are met with an ominous forecast: Mt. Etna has “spewed a plume of ash and gas,” a lunar eclipse is imminent, and the Levante, a strong easterly wind, will soon blow in. Amid the ever-shifting atmosphere, mother and daughter each search for “the chance to begin, or to begin again.” The novel was excerpted in the magazine. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Renoir Girls by Catherine Ostler (Atria)Nonfiction This sweeping biography of the daughters of a French Jewish banking dynasty—who were painted by Renoir, and counted Proust as a family friend—unfolds in parallel worlds: a glittering Paris of privilege, and a Paris where widespread poverty and political instability fuelled profound social anxiety. Ostler traces a thread of anti-Jewish hatred through both worlds, as she illustrates how the sisters’ rarefied existence was frequently marred by bursts of prejudice. In 1882, shortly after completing the girls’ portraits, for instance, Renoir declared that he was “washing my hands of the Jews.” As Ostler shows, his stated reasons were vague and irrelevant. Renoir was merely a “cork in the current” of antisemitism. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Air by Christian Kracht, translated from the German by Daniel Bowles (Liveright)Fiction Two story lines anchor this novel: one centered on a present-day designer with a Luddism-inflected aesthetic, and one that takes place in a fantastical realm where a young girl accidentally shoots a man she has mistaken for a deer. In the first plot, the designer disappears during a solar storm while working on a project in Norway. In the second, the girl and the man run from soldiers sent by a malevolent ruler. In that reality, people live on what they forage and kill; they wear shared clothes; they don’t have inventions like mirrors or—crucially—antibiotics. Though this world lacks the twenty-first-century trappings that so bothered the designer, its brutalities also suggest that nostalgia for the pre-modern is a knife that cuts both ways. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### I Want You to Be Happy by Jem Calder (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction “A new person finding you interesting makes you feel new.” So reflects one of the protagonists of this intimate novel, which follows the relationship between two creative aspirants in London—a young woman working as a barista while nursing dreams of poetry, and a slightly older man who is a copywriter, but hopes to become a novelist. The two meet at a bar one night, then go home together. As Calder tracks the course of their romance, from the careful texting of its early days to reckonings with the characters’ darker elements—the copywriter, it emerges, drinks excessively—he gives the perennial human features of self-sabotage and solipsism a fresh look. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Miraculous Season by V. R. “Bunny” Lang (New York Review Books)Poetry The American poet Violet Ranney Lang was born in 1924 and died in 1956, of Hodgkin’s lymphoma, at the age of thirty-two. She may have been cut off in her prime, but her prime is indisputably her own. Lang produced poems with a singular blend of severity and skittishness. In her tart, forbidding lines, she comes across as both quite at ease in aristocratic settings (she was a débutante born in Boston, to old money) and all too eager to smash their social rules. “The Miraculous Season,” which was first published in the U.K., in 2024, gathers some of the poetry she produced as a serious young writer, when she studied at Harvard, befriended Frank O’Hara, wrote and directed and performed in plays, and, finally, squared up to the facts of death as she had to the facts of her life—with cheerfully desperate bravado. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “A Forgotten Queen Bee of Modern Poetry,” by Anthony Lane

### Glyph by Ali Smith (Pantheon)Fiction Continuing its decorated author’s project of devising a contemporary language for fiction while revisiting the past, this novel follows two sisters, Patricia and Petra, long estranged, who are haunted by stories from their childhood: one of a man who was shot during the First World War, and the other of a person who met a gruesome death in the Second. Amid the disappointments of the present—oppressive digital technology and work uncertainty—ghosts and shared recollections bring the sisters together, and closer to Patricia’s adopted daughter, Bill, who represents both the pessimism and the idealism of a younger generation. Animated by dialogue and wordplay, Smith’s novel shines with her intuition, and her ability to surprise. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead (Doubleday)Fiction In the gripping conclusion of his New York crime trilogy, Whitehead takes us to early nineteen-eighties Harlem, where the protagonist Ray Carney, like the entire city, seems to be on the rise. New York is recovering from near-bankruptcy, roused by the promise of Reaganomics; Carney has been named Dealer of the Month at his furniture store and plans to abandon the brutal criminality that’s plagued his family for generations—after one more heist. Hoping to help his wife start a business, he mixes with a master malefactor and is plunged back into the city’s felonious landscape. His devotion to his spouse, allegiance to a dangerous old accomplice, and grief over the murder of his cousin threaten an existence he has spent years building. Whitehead, a winner of two Pulitzer Prizes, gives the Harlem Trilogy a finale that pays haunting homage to the imperfect city where he and his characters are perpetually reinvented. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Colson Whitehead’s Big Score,” by Julian Lucas

### Élisabeth by Éric Rohmer, translated from the French by Aaron Kerner (McNally Editions)Fiction Constructed as a set of ruses and evasions, “Élisabeth” was the only novel that the great French New Wave filmmaker Rohmer ever wrote. Completed in the summer of 1944, amid battles for the liberation of Paris from Nazi occupiers, the book’s narrative begins in 1939, with characters anticipating the end of summer and a return to business as usual in the fall, unaware of what is to come. “Élisabeth” depicts a social world that manages to survive cataclysm: even during the Occupation, people go to college, hold jobs, take vacations, flirt, marry, separate, and write. Its central character, Michel, is an engineer in his early twenties who is having doubts about his engagement to a woman named Irène, a widow a few years older than he. As Rohmer pursues this through line, he flits from character to character, location to location, assembling a book that is ultimately an exemplary modernist novel. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Éric Rohmer’s Novel “Élisabeth” Is a Precocious Literary Triumph,” by Richard Brody

### The Cruelty of Nice Folks by Justin Ellis (Harper)Nonfiction Minneapolis has long been a stronghold of progressivism: slavery was banned there upon Minnesota’s statehood, and it was an early adopter of public housing. But, as Ellis demonstrates in this survey of the city’s racial history, liberal policy achievements tend to obscure more insidious forms of exclusion. A Minneapolis native, Ellis returns to his home after the murder of George Floyd. His resulting exploration tracks the ways in which Black residents were effectively segregated, through racial covenants and redlining, and overpoliced. Though Ellis’s long view of the city is tinged with cynicism, its response to last winter’s ICE invasion creates, he contends, an opening for hope. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Death of the Soccer God by Dimitry Elias Léger (MCD x FSG)Fiction This stylish historical picaresque examines Haitian identity and history by recounting the “brief, wondrous life” of a fictional athlete, Gilbert Chevalier. Born to a wealthy family in Port-au-Prince, the young Chevalier has a prodigious talent for soccer. When he’s dispatched to Columbia University for college, he rooms with Miles Davis, consorts with John Coltrane, and is recruited to play for the United States in the 1950 World Cup, in Brazil. There he meets a nine-year-old Pelé and leads the American team to a stunning upset of England. Returning to Haiti after playing professional football in Europe, Chevalier runs afoul of President François Duvalier—an incident with dangerous consequences. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### They Stole a City by Lauren Collins (Penguin Press)Nonfiction In this gripping narrative, part history and part reportage, Collins, a staff writer, returns to her home town of Wilmington, North Carolina, to explore a chapter in the city’s history that was long overlooked or actively suppressed: in November, 1898, a mob of white supremacists rampaged through the streets, killing Black people and seizing the city government in what is thought to be the only successful coup d’état on American soil. The book, which was excerpted in *The New Yorker*, describes how the violence reverberated through generations of Wilmington families, shaping lives in ways that official histories failed to acknowledge. The racist takeover of the city happened more than a century ago, yet its lessons are urgent as ever, Collins writes: “There is no more explicit example of the vulnerability of American democracy, and of the magnitude of the task of repairing it once it is breached.”

blocks.text: Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

items: ### Spawning Season by Joseph Osmundson (Bloomsbury)Nonfiction Anchored by a poignant account of his efforts to become a father, this memoir, by a microbiologist, is also a wide-ranging meditation on what it means to be biologically “fit” in Western society today. Though the barriers to parenthood which Osmundson encounters don’t exist for all of us (he’s queer; he’s male; he’s not able to afford surrogacy or adoption), his emotional journey will be instantly recognizable to anyone whose dreams of having a child have been dashed or deferred. Some of that arc is grappling with various reasons not to have a child, including climate change. A secondary narrative, following salmon on their journey to reproduce in warming waters, proves surprisingly apposite, partly thanks to Osmundson’s expertise on the subject, and partly because it underscores what is uniquely human about his dilemma: that, for us, a universal instinct can also be a question. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Perfect Moment by Isaac Butler (Bloomsbury)Nonfiction In this lively history, Butler revisits the American culture wars that started in the late nineteen-eighties, chronicling how cöordinated conservative campaigns transformed obscure disputes over federal museum grants into defining battles for the soul of the Republican Party. Along the way, indelible scenes of senators ripping exhibition catalogues and inviting “women and children” to leave the Senate chamber before brandishing Robert Mapplethorpe’s photographs lend the political history novelistic propulsion. The culture wars, Butler suggests, are less a closed chapter than a continuing conflict: if “the culture wars of the late twentieth century were the World War I of American arts and letters,” he writes, “we have now entered World War II.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “How “Piss Christ” Became a Culture-War Bomb,” by Louis Menand

### Nebraska by Monica Datta (Astra)Fiction This ambitious novel springs from a moment of apparent inhuman cruelty: a mother, Anna Chatterjee, kills her disabled son, pushing his wheelchair in front of an oncoming train. The murder and its fraught causes are recounted by a Bengali analyst, who is himself interpreting them from the records of a different analyst with connections to Chatterjee’s two living children. When these two children, along with Chatterjee’s husband, attempt to pick her up at the end of her prison sentence, they find she is already gone. Datta explores the impact of enormous colonial forces on the unconscious of a single individual, her narrative shifting between time lines and continents in a performance that is both dizzying and energizing. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Axe in Blossom by Franz Wright (Knopf)Poetry Wright, who died in 2015, composed these poems while suffering from lung cancer, recording many of them in scribbles around his apartment in Waltham, Massachusetts. And yet his condition is never an occasion for self-pity; his lines glow, instead, with the light of honesty and self-deprecation. He remarks on his “odd-sounding croak that was once a good voice”; at another point, spotting his reflection in a bus, he writes, “I looked like a suicide / returning an overdue book to the library.” Wright has a gift for tender, wisecracking moments, and he renders them with extraordinary sensory detail, whether he’s observing something as close as a fly or as distant as the stars. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “A Dying Poet’s Farewell to the World,” by Dan Chiasson

### Muskism by Quinn SlobodianBen Tarnoff (Harper)Nonfiction What is the philosophy that underpins Elon Musk’s varied ventures, from Tesla to SpaceX to DOGE? The answer, this slim study contends, is a creed in which “states and individuals” can achieve “sovereignty through technology.” The portrait of Musk that emerges here is that of a childish, terminally online man who desires to eliminate the messiness of contemporary life for a more rigid order. “To say that Muskism is worth taking seriously is not to say that its success is guaranteed,” Slobodian and Tarnoff write. But the “institutional breakdown” of the twenty-first century, they warn, could mean that Muskism will profoundly shape the world to come. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### You Won’t Get Free of It by Rachel Aviv (Knopf)Nonfiction In a collection of pieces, most originally written for *The New Yorker* and now recast, Aviv examines maternal relationships across an array of charged situations, including the story of a Filipina nanny in the United States who has not seen her own children in years, and that of the writer Alice Munro, whose husband sexually abused one of her daughters. Aviv, a staff writer at the magazine, explores the limits of what the family structure can reveal and conceal.

items: ### The Infinity Machine by Sebastian Mallaby (Penguin)Nonfiction Demis Hassabis long dreamed of building a machine powerful enough to untangle science’s greatest mysteries. In 2010, at the age of thirty-four, he co-founded the A.I. startup DeepMind to pursue this vision. Since then, the company’s creations have solved painfully difficult problems in fields from mathematics to computational biology. One of its programs produced a solution to the so-called protein-folding problem, representing a dramatic advance in the science of drug discovery and bringing Hassabis a Nobel Prize. Mallaby, a longtime financial journalist, is a nimble storyteller, and his portrait of one of the single-minded personalities plunging the world into an uncertain future is also an engaging drama of discovery. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### While We Were Waiting by Katherine Nouri Hughes (Delphinium)Fiction In this harrowing novel, two families pass long, uncertain hours in the waiting rooms of a Manhattan hospital. A venture capitalist who assesses risk for a living is helpless as his wife, beset by preeclampsia, is rushed to an emergency delivery. Nearby sits a family of Chaldean Christians exiled from Iraq—an anxious archeologist, his pregnant radiologist wife, and his imperious mother, who bought a bulletproof Maybach to transport her daughter-in-law to the hospital for the delivery. Hughes, an American writer of Iraqi and Irish descent, has an acute ear for the half spoken, whether in a doctor’s clipped bulletins or a husband’s misfired word. The novel dwells in the porous hours of waiting—the interstices in which, as the title suggests, life accrues. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Morbid by Saul Justin Newman (M.I.T.)Nonfiction In 2024, Newman, an interdisciplinary scholar at Oxford, won the satirical Ig Nobel Prize for demonstrating that many of the world’s oldest living people may actually be dead. In some cases, families pretended that a relative was still alive so that they could continue collecting pension checks. In other cases, living individuals exaggerated their ages so much that they were falsely deemed centenarians. In this lively and sometimes conspiratorial new volume, Newman argues convincingly that such instances of fraud are far more common than longevity gurus like to admit. In his telling, they represent “a systematic disaster” that undermines the science of aging and contributes to all manner of misguided health fads. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Something Is Very Wrong with Modern Longevity Science,” by Dhruv Khullar

### If This Be Magic by Daniel Hahn (Knopf)Nonfiction This rich and often funny book, by a translator of Portuguese, Spanish, and French, investigates one of literature’s most challenging endeavors: replacing every word in a Shakespeare play with words from another language while having the result remain the Bard. Through interviews with translators and side-by-side comparisons of text, Hahn examines the many problems that translators face. (In Italian, for instance, far fewer common words are monosyllabic than in English, so a translated Shakespeare risks growing much longer than the original.) While exploring questions about ambiguity, order, pronouns, and even the use of A.I., Hahn’s study of literary translation widens into a reflection on the broader mysteries of language. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Sexual Evolution by Nathan H. Lents (Mariner)Nonfiction Lents, a biology professor at John Jay College, examines some of the natural world’s most sexually bewildering characters—from earthworms, which are hermaphroditic and mutually inseminate each other, to bluegill sunfish, which sometimes work as a two-male-one-female throuple to reproduce. Lents argues that the surge in sexual experimentation among humans is a way of reclaiming the expansive relationship with sex that other life forms have long indulged in. Why animals have sex, and in such creative ways, is still something of an evolutionary puzzle, and Lents doesn’t attempt to solve it. But he does encourage sexual curiosity and a healthy skepticism of norms, pointing out that, if “Finding Nemo” represented its clownfish accurately, Nemo’s dad would have become female after losing his missus, and then mated with his son. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “What’s the Point of Sex, Anyway?,” by Elizabeth Kolbert

### A Terrible Intimacy by Melvin Patrick Ely (Holt)Nonfiction This history, by a Bancroft Prize winner, analyzes six trials that took place in Prince Edward County, Virginia, between 1825 and 1861, illuminating the complexity of interracial relationships in the slaveholding South. Ely calls upon a wide range of sources to illustrate the ways in which physical proximity between enslavers and enslaved people created “crosscurrents of community life,” including moments of recreation, socializing, trade, and sex. His most compelling observations arise from smaller details he teases out of the trials’ testimony, which capture the texture of the everyday—from how people travelled at night to the manner in which they kept time. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Whistler by Ann Patchett (Harper)Fiction When Daphne, the middle-aged narrator of this pensive novel, was a child, she developed a precious bond with Eddie, her stepfather. But, after the pair got into a car accident, Daphne’s mother divorced Eddie, alleging that he was negligent, and then cut him off entirely. Daphne “put the whole thing”—her memories of Eddie, and of that night—“in a box.” For nearly half a century, she left those thoughts untouched. Then Daphne and Eddie run into each other, and, despite all the time that has passed, Daphne finds that the two are still profoundly connected. Together, she and Eddie face their respective pasts, untangling the feelings of betrayal, regret, and love that emerge in the process. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

From Our Pages ### The Frenzy by Joyce Carol Oates (Hogarth)Fiction In her latest collection of stories, Oates explores moments of change and crisis in the lives of her characters, who behave violently, childishly, unpredictably, cravenly, or, occasionally, bravely when they find themselves in situations they can’t entirely control. The first line of the book’s title story, which is one of two that appeared first in *The New Yorker*—“Is the irrevocable, unforgivable act behind him, or ahead?”—could open almost any piece in this collection. The question is not if but when, and what the fallout of that act will be. Oates answers these questions in breathless, visceral prose that matches the definition of literature she gave in a Q. and A. for the magazine: “a texture of words evoking life in the most vivid ways—psychologically, physically.”

items: ### Newcomers by Alan Mikhail (Liveright)Nonfiction In this short but powerful biography, Mikhail investigates the lives of Anthony Jansen van Salee and his wife, Grietje Reyniers, who rose from obscure origins—Mikhail speculates that Salee was a freed slave; Reyniers was a barmaid and sex worker—to become one of New Netherland’s founding families. Regarded by their fellow-colonists as “sinful moral outsiders,” van Salee and Reyniers were banished from the colony’s mainstay on Manhattan and forced to live on Long Island. It was there, by means of a war that the colony waged on Native people, that the couple forged new reputations as defenders and “anchors” of Dutch settlement, accruing property, hiring laborers, and joining the ranks of the landed élite. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Nonstop Bodies by Rennie McDougall (Abrams)Nonfiction In this new history, McDougall, an arts journalist, revisits the twentieth century, a particularly dance-rich time in New York City, with an eye to the social and cultural context in which dancing occurs. “Dance history,” he writes, “often maintains a separation between ‘high’ and ‘low.’ ” In “Nonstop Bodies,” he attempts to overcome this divide, placing modern dance pioneers, such as Martha Graham, side by side with the more democratic, but no less fertile, creativity of the people who invented the city’s iconic dances. The Lindy Hop, an inventive, joyfully virtuosic dance to jazz, was developed during the Harlem Renaissance. The dance, McDougall writes, “actively rejected the idea of individual creators,” revelling instead in the inventions of each dancer, each couple, who contributed to an ever-expanding pool of ideas about movement, which subsequently became available to all. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “When Dance in New York Took Center Stage,” by Marina Harss

### Ghost-Eye by Amitav Ghosh (Farrar, Straus & Giroux)Fiction This sweeping novel opens in nineteen-sixties Calcutta, when a three-year-old girl demands to eat fish, shocking her family of Jains. Disturbed, her parents summon a psychologist, who concludes that she is the reincarnation of a person who grew up in a fishing village in the Sundarban forests, to the southeast. Fifty years later, an energy corporation announces plans to build a plant in that area, threatening ecological devastation. The psychologist’s adult nephew has been recruited by an environmentalist who believes that the psychologist’s case files hold the key to saving the forest. The story—replete with history and science, spiritualism and synchronicities—suggests that to find salvation, we must “remind ourselves of the old ways.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Yuppies by Dylan Gottlieb (Harvard)Nonfiction “Yuppies” examines the men and women employed in the intertwined fields of finance and Big Law in nineteen-eighties New York. The book’s “precipitating event,” Gottlieb writes, is “the unshackling of Wall Street during the Carter and Reagan administrations,” when the prospect of high-paying jobs drew legions of ambitious young people to New York. “In 1979, only one in thirty seniors at the University of Pennsylvania headed to Wall Street,” Gottlieb reports. “By 1987, it was one in three.” Eschewing pop-sociological clichés, he focusses on the thing that defined yuppies more deeply than their fondness for Chardonnay or sushi: their work. Career, for his subjects, was a life style, an ethos of striving and competition which defined their professional lives, pervaded their leisure hours, and reshaped the American economy. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “When Did White-Collar Work Start to Look So Bleak?,” by Molly Fischer

From Our Pages ### Baby in a Box by Sarah Braunstein (Norton)Fiction The first collection of stories by Braunstein grapples with relationships of care. A motel housekeeper and a guest, a single mother and her child, teen-age best friends—these dynamics and others are examined in idiosyncratic, sidelong ways. The stories, four of which appeared in the magazine, are strange, sly, and funny. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Once upon a Time There Was Truth by Jack Zipes (Yale)Nonfiction Zipes, an accomplished scholar of fairy tales, explores the genre’s enduring appeal and its social functions in this erudite essay collection. He acknowledges the long global history of folk stories, but focusses on the Western “literary” fairy tale, charting its emergence out of oral tradition—aided by the printing press, the standardization of vernacular languages, and the rise of modern nation-states—and the process by which it became oriented primarily toward children. Examining both classics (“Hansel and Gretel”) and commercial empires (Disney), Zipes illuminates the fairy tale’s often contradictory tendencies, among them its propagation of conformist values along with its subversive potential, and its power to either “domesticate the imagination” or liberate it. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Lost Soldiers by Andrey Kurkov, translated from the Russian by Boris Dralyuk (HarperVia)Fiction In this madcap detective story, Samson Kolechko, a young investigator in Kyiv, is assigned a seemingly impossible case. The year is 1919, the midst of Bolshevik takeover in Ukraine, and twenty-eight Red Army soldiers have vanished into thin air, last seen at a bathhouse. Kolechko must track them down. He gets little help from the absurd locals, who range from obstinately useless to selfishly malicious. Kolechko is a kind of anti-Poirot—a fairly conventional man whose powers of detection lie not in a dazzling intuition but in a supernatural severed ear, which has a bug-like ability to pick up dialogue. In Kurkov’s hands, his efforts offer both serious meditations and page-turning diversion. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Radical Duke by Danielle Allen (Liveright)Nonfiction Charles Lennox, the third Duke of Richmond, rarely gets more than a footnote in history books. When he is remembered at all, it’s for his beauty, appetite, Sèvres porcelain, and radical politics. Then Allen, a political-philosophy professor at Harvard, found an early copy of the Declaration of Independence in Sussex, England, that had once belonged to Richmond. Her discovery led to this biography, which revises the familiar story of American independence as an American achievement alone. Allen argues that the Revolution was also charged by Richmond’s criticisms of the Crown and advocacy for democratic equality across the Atlantic. A confidant and collaborator of Thomas Paine, Richmond was among the first members of England’s élite to champion freedom of the press, religious liberty, and universal male suffrage. “Radical Duke” makes a vigorous case for Richmond as a neglected founder whose ideas helped propel the colonists’ rebellion and anticipated modern democratic representation. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Did a Rowdy English Nobleman Mastermind the American Revolution?,” by Adam Gopnik

### My World Is Melting by Line Nagell Ylvisåker, translated from the Norwegian by Kelsey Camacho (Wisconsin)Nonfiction The islands of Svalbard are the world’s northernmost inhabited region; they are also experiencing climate change at an accelerated pace. In this memoir, Ylvisåker, who is from Longyearbyen, a small town in the archipelago which was hit by a deadly avalanche in 2015, documents Svalbard’s transformation. She interviews a trapper who testifies to the changing patterns of the native animals he has interacted with over the past half century, and shows locals struggling with the pressures of a “last-chance tourism” boom. Her portrait of residents pinched between floods and receding sea ice is a testament to their love of this vulnerable land that is their home. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Homebound by Portia Elan (Scribner)Fiction This imaginative début novel takes place in two settings: Cincinnati, in the nineteen-eighties; and a flooded world, six hundred years later. In the latter time line, Yesiko, a middle-aged ship captain who is burdened by medical debt, picks up some mysterious passengers—including a moody robot—who promise to pay handsomely. In Cincinnati, a teen-ager named Beck ponders an unfinished video game designed by her late uncle, who has died of an H.I.V.-like disease. At once a work of dystopian science fiction and a tale of lesbian self-discovery, the novel is ultimately concerned with “what it means to show up even when you’re afraid.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Land by Maggie O’Farrell (Knopf)Fiction Cartography serves as both narrative engine and theme in “Land,” a new historical novel by the author of “Hamnet.” A central figure, Tomás, is a skilled laborer in eighteen-sixties Ireland, tasked with making maps for the British, who are occupying the country. He wants to depict not only relevant topographical features and place names but also the ravages of the Great Hunger, which killed twelve per cent of the population and led two million more to emigrate. Through its characters, the book stages an argument about the virtues of various types of maps—those measured, those recollected, those dreamed up. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Maggie O’Farrell and the Art of Inventing the Past,” by Katy Waldman

### This Vast Enterprise by Craig Fehrman (Avid Reader)Nonfiction History is usually written in the third person, even though it has to be lived in the first, and Fehrman takes advantage of the rich and deep documentation of the Lewis and Clark expedition to try to reconcile the discrepancy. The book adopts the perspectives not only of Lewis and of Clark but also of other members of the expedition, including an enslaved Black man named York, whom Clark brought along as a personal servant, and of five Native Americans whom the explorers encountered. Fehrman doesn’t attempt to speak in the voices of his subjects. He merely focusses on what each individual experienced and knew, while keeping in mind how much they didn’t experience or know—an analytic technique that historians have always been free to borrow from novelists but which they often lose sight of in the scramble to accumulate data. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “Looking Back at Lewis and Clark,” by Caleb Crain

### Adrift in the South by Xiao Hai, translated from the Chinese by Tony Hao (Granta)Nonfiction At fifteen, the writer Xiao Hai left his home town to find work in the factories of southern China. This deeply affecting memoir, which is strung like a wire between the alienation of the assembly line and the dignifying promise of literature, documents his experience. Hai first began to write short verses from the production floor of a garment factory, where, tasked with stitching patterns onto athletic jerseys, he was overcome by feelings that he struggled to name. By the time he moved to a village in Beijing, about a decade later, he had amassed a trove of some four hundred poems. “I always returned to my dorm with a little strength left,” Hai recounts, “and with that strength I dreamed the simplest, most sincere, most fervid dreams.” Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### Magadh by Shrikant Verma, translated from the Hindi by Rahul Soni (Liveright)Poetry The title of this collection, first published in 1984, and written by a central figure of the modernist Nayi Kavita (New Poetry) movement, refers to an ancient kingdom that looms large in Indian history and myth. Verma, who also served as a member of Parliament, renders Magadh as a place at once real and imaginary, lasting and lost—both a point of origin and an unreachable destination. The book circles political concerns that remain relevant today, including empire, caste prejudice, and the dangers of despotism and corruption. But in Soni’s careful translation, the repetitions and subtle variation of Verma’s poems also achieve a haunting, transcendental resonance. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshop

### The Dog’s Gaze by Thomas W. Laqueur (Penguin Press)Nonfiction A dog’s gaze is both omniscient and deeply innocent. It longs to be made into art—and, for centuries, dogs have been. Laqueur, a historian at the University of California, Berkeley, looks back at the canines immortalized in visual art work and considers how they help us see ourselves. We bred dogs, then illustrated them, to be affectionate, trustworthy witnesses to the human condition; they hunt beside us, like the hounds of Bruegel the Elder’s “The Hunters in the Snow,” and complete our homes, like the gray mutt curled on a blanket in Matisse’s “Interior with a Dog.” Far from the wolves from which they evolved, dogs possess and convey the emotions that humans value in each other, reminding us of our humanity when we need it most. And yet, Laqueur argues, their undying companionship and captivating stare is unlike anything we’ve ever found in our own species. Buy from Barnes & NobleAmazonBookshopRead more: “What Dogs See When They Look at Us,” by Adam Gopnik

### The Story of Birds by Steve Brusatte (Mariner)Nonfiction As this natural history points out, birds are dinosaurs—the only ones who survived the last extinction event. A single Jurassic species, *Archaeopteryx*, is the reptilian ancestor of all birds today, from the flightless, kickboxing cassowary to the penguins who fly underwater. Brusatte, a renowned paleontologist, leads readers through time in a series of vignettes—a predator hunt with an apocalyptic Cretaceous backdrop, a mating ritual between water birds, a monster preying on a marsupial just fifteen million years ago—and pairs them with fossil discoveries that detail their evolutionary past. Throughout, academic precision gives way to sheer delight over these animals, and their song and flight.
